div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
Mt DEAREST NErs.TE,

Isn't this a lovely summer? I'm so glad it is, because the shirts are being worn more than ever. They seem to be more popular than they have ever been before. The favourite material is cotton, either striped, figured, or plain, as suits the taste of the wearer. Silk is not largely used for shirts. The styles of making are similar to those of last year, but, of course, manufacturers each year place something new upon the market to take the public fancy. This summer the shirt must have a blouse front; also a yoke in the back with a' slight full- ness gathered into belt. The collar is cut with deep points in front, and the cuffs are deep and fastened with link buttons. The sleeves are full, yet not too full to wear inside the jacket sleeve. But even then they can be as large as one may desire, for jacket sleeves are as immense as are all sleeves nowadays. The belt is of the same material as the shirt, but usu:illy the silk belts with fancy buckles and belt pins are worn instead of the ones supplied with the shirt. Shirts wash well if made of a good material, and they look nice until worn out. They are also cool, and can be worn with any skirt. And last, and by no means least, they are inexpensive. These three 'recom- mendations should insure their ' popularity for an indefinite period. I said that cotton was the favourite material, but for those who can afford it silk and flannel are quite as much worn. One made in this former material, but which would do equally well in the latter, was made with blouse front, stand-up collar, and full bishop sleeves, and had paste studs. The toque worn with this costume was of accordion- pleated lace, with pink roses and foliage. Them were satin ribbon bows.

a very . in matters feminine, that is to say, dressy. This year what I noticed specially was the head-gear, some of which was very tempting. For instance, a pure white hat made of the light fancy straw so much in vogue was all a-foam with white chiffon and feathers on the top. A Panama straw in a delicate biscuit colour looked deliciously cool with its trimming of pale green, heliotrope, y ellow and white flowers. Another lovely hat was in the finest Dunstable straw, curved about in an indescribable fashion which made it marvellously becoming. It was trimmed with four exquisite, large pink roses, of the kind whose petals curl back in a paler pink. I forget their name, only remembering that it is quite unworthy of them. A small rose ander the brim rests on the hair with a puff of white chiffon. The crown, made of the straw like the brim, is high, and juts slightly outwards at the very top, like those of the peaked hats that Prussian soldiers wear at this day. An aigrette of black feathers throws all the white softness of the chiffon and the tender pink of the roses into better relief.

The butter-coloured straw that is used so largely for hats takes my fancy greatly. One made of this material was a neat shape, with low crown, slightly turned up at the back, and with slightly drooping aides. It was edged under the brim with black fancy straw, and trimmed with blue shot glace sill: bows, veiled with fine black lace, two black wings and tinted foliage resting on the hair. This hat would suit most kinds of faces.

css colour;. I may tell yo, then, that 'White is being much worn as a trimming, or, should I say, as a finish to dresses; and the effect is collectively pretty and bright in the extreme, while individually it is charmingly becoming. Smart crepon gowns in the newest shades of blue and green have folded collars of white satin with rosettes at either side, and the sleeves are similarly finished off at the wrist. Then there are white collars, often like those of sailors', in white muslin and lace; while many pretty afternoon frocks have white satin and moire collars cut deep and square at the back like that on the jacket of an able-bodied seaman, and finished with applied lace or embroidery. Blue is the favourite colour, in all the shades of corn- flower possible to conjecture; that of flax-flower, which is somewhat deeper than lavender' and also with several degrees more of a violet shade in it, is about the most recent development of the craze for this colour.

a.attle children look j pretty in the fashion- able pe.lisis. A ilulightful one for a little girl may be made of soft cream silk, with frills of silk lace and gimp. There is also a silk hood, with embroidered crown, and a rustic bebe ribbon in the front.
Your loving JENNii.

Madame Patti's Earnings. Now that Mme. Patti is almost sharing the honours with Mr. W. G. Grace, it is interesting to note the re- sults of some of her early innings. From the first she seems to have what had one may call a very fair living' wage though it was years later that " Patti terms" were asked and paid. She was engaged for five years by Mr. Strakosch, when she made her debut in New York, at a progressive salary, which began at £BO a month for the first year, rose to £l2O for the second, and £l6O for the third, and culminated in £2OO for the fourth and fifth. Her five years' engagement in London with Mr. Gye, which began when she was a girl of eighteen, was at practically double the terms—£lBo a month for the first year, then £2OO, £250, £290, and finally £4OO, two performances a week to be given. £BOO for three songs is nearer the figure now.

div.head: Women and Work.
div.p: Women and Work.

So the cry that women are flooding the labour market and driving out men has apparently no ground ! Miss Collett, in her interesting report to the Board of Trade on the employment of women, declares that in the ten years taken from 1881.91 the proportion of women re- turned as occupied remains practically stationary. In 1881, in every one hundred women and girls over ten , years 34.05 were returned as occupied, and in 1891 '3442. The employment of -narried and elderly women has, on the whole, diminished, and the employment of women in casual occupations has declined. On the other hand, there has been an increase in the employ- ment of women and girls under twenty-five, although this holds good with regard to young men and boys. The women workers in the North of England are, in- dustrially far ahead of those in the South. The textile trades offer such high wages to women that the Northern women do not regard employment merely as a means of livelihood before marriage; they regard it as their occu- pation in life far more than domestic management. In the South, where factory industries are small, the work. ing girls merely take up work for a time, and look for- ward to marriage to release them from industry. The result is that the girl rarely aims at becoming an effici- ent worker, and, in case of the death or breakdown of her husband, the woman is practically helpless. Another interesting point is that whilst the working- class women are more and more tending to remain at home with the increase in the husband's earnings, amongst middle-class girls there is greater tendency to go out into the world to make a way for themselves. Another interesting fact is that a higher standard of comfort has both increased and decreased the employ- ment of women. Ia the middle class the high standard of comfort, the smaller field for dcmestic usefulness, a diminished chance of marrying, and apprehension for the future have encouraged the entrance of girls into the labour market ; whilst in the working-class, with in- creasing prosperity and a rising standard of comfort, there is a general feeling for the services of the wife at least, and, when possible, the daughters also, to be re- tained at home.

div.head: Warning for Women:
div.p: A Warning for Women:

_ Many women, young girls in particular, have a bad habit of chewing their hair. This practice is not only disgusting but dangerous. A few weeks ago a young woman was received at the South Devon and East Corn- wall Hospital. When a..?mitted she was supposed to be suffering from a large abdominal tumour. An examin- ation by Dr. Paul Swain resulted in his opening her stomach, from whence he succeeded in extracting, a mass of hair weighing no less than 51b. 3-z. The wound was sown up and the patient rallied, ultimately recover- ing, thanks to the skill of Dr. Swain. The girl ackr.ow- ledged that she had been in the habit some time ago of chewing small quantities of her hair. The mass ex- tracted is now in the Museum of the Royal College of Surgeons.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, J ULY 6. 1895.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, J ULY 6. 1895.

JSut nis lire witn Isabel nad been so blisstul, anis he had felt such a desolation when she was taken from him, that his heart seemed to yearn for com- panionship; and with that feeling upon him Lady Travers found him. But her whole game wasn't played when she had won his hand and his name. She wanted something for her son. "This Captain Harold Travers was a man very much after his father's stamp. He was reckless and heartless, and had enough of polish to make his way in society. He went at work upon Sir John's good graces and found his way into them. And when his lordship prepared for his return to England he allowed the captain to sell his com- mission and bear him company. And he did more: He allowed Harold to drop the name of Travers and to take that of Berwick in its place, thus recognising him as an adopted son. You must un- derstand that Sir John was now past sixty, and more easily worked upon than formerly. He fancied that he was never so firm of will, and never so independent; but there was one at the helm that knew how to govern him. "When his lordship, with his new family, reached home, Arthur had grown to be a youth of sixteen, and he was acknowledged by all who knew him to be the handsomest, and the bravest, and the strongest boy of his years in our riding. He had cut up some wild pranks, to be sure, but nothing that came of an evil disposition. The new Lady Birchmear pretended a strong love for him; and Harold was openly very kind to him. Within a few months after Sir John's return Arthur was sent away to school at Oxford; and there he has beau most of the time until three months ago' when he came home with the resolution to study no more. "At first Sir John had only planned that Arthur should pursue a course of study that would fit him for public political life, and then we fancied that he meant to make the lad his heir—for you will understand that his lordship has had no children of his own—but after a time, in three years from the -'

ad's first entrance at college, Sir Jorm changed the plan, and wanted him to prepare for the church. *When the old servants heard of this—and they heard of it when Arthur came home at vacation— they were sure that Lady Birchtnear had been at work, and that the son of Isabel Raiasford was not sure of inh-titing the manor. However, Arthur resolved that he would not be a churchman, and when Sir Jottu was satisfied that his op- position could not be overcome, he proposed the bar instead. But the youth would • -not have that either. He would enter the army. In fact, it was his earnest wish to join the army, and he once said to me, said he: Peter, when my school-days are over I shall go into the army. I would rather go in as a private, and carry a musket and a knapsack, than be a hanger-on at this place, and in this company.' I knew very well what he meant. I knew that he knew that Lady l3irchmear hated him, and that Harold, with all his smiling surface, was bitterly jealous of him. "But I won't spin it out longer than I can help. Three months ago Atrthur came home from college, and he came home in debt. He had been wild and extravagant. Sir John paid his debts, and gave him a lecture. Arthur knew that some one had been undermining him, and he took the lecture badly. After that he asked his lordship to buy him a commission in a regiment which had just been ordered to India. Sir John didn't flatly refuse, nor did he give his assent; but he gave another lecture, which the lad took with very ill grace, and he took it thus because he knew that her ladyship was at the bottom of it." " But," suggested Jason Smart, "if I under- stand you aright, both Lady Helen and her son Harold are eager to get rid of this young man r " Yes, so they are." "And they have influence with Sir John ?" "They Seem to have about as much as they choose to exercise." "Then why don't they urge his joining the army? How could they be rid of him more surely than by sending him off to fight the Hindoo bar- barians ?" The old keeper nodded mysteriously, and laid his finger very quietly upon the other's hand, as he reptied "Be sure they'll recommend the commission when they're ready for it. They know that Arthur is brave and generous, and that he is already a soldier. He was accounted the best swordsman, and the best shot, and the best boxer, at Oxford, ' and that is saying a great deal. They know all this and they may fear that if he were to go away now he might take much of the old lord's good-will and good wishes with him, which they don't want him to do." "Mercy on me I Do you mean, Peter, that—* "I mean," said the keeper, as Jason hesitated, "that they are bound to ruin Arthur in Sir John's estimation if they can. You must remember that the baron is almost seventy, and that he is not so strong as he was once. Remember, also, that her ladyship is yet in the prime of life, with- her wonderful energies unimpaired; and, remember furthermore, that Harold Berwick, as he now bears his name, is a crafty, heartless, scheming man of the world, with large experience, and a few

This is a story of love and war, and is full of adventures in the Highlands of Scotland, on the sea, and in the jungles of India. It is intensely interesting from the first to the last.

div.head: CHAPTER I.
div.p: CHAPTER I.

A YAMILY STORY. The 7.llanor of Birchmear was one of the oldest and most extensive in England. It had been the seat of the Barons Birchmear for centuries, the first lord of the demesne having received his patent from Henry 111. During the reign of Elizabeth, one Reginald Berwick, a brave and loyal knight, had come by marriage to the estate and to the peerage, since which time this family, with enduring vitality in the male line had held itself upon record, and the Berwicks had been Barons Birch- mear of Birchmear down to the present. The mansion, or manor-house' was a grand old castellated pile, with as many different styles of architecture in its rambling parts as there had been periods of masonic progress during its youth, and the outcroppings of these various periods were consecutively recognisable. Even the donjon and the tower of the time of the First Edward had been well preserved, and the additions of modern date were of a high standard of taste and excellence. The domain was ample. There were fair lawns and gardens, and extensive p4rks and preserves, broad meadows and fruitful slopes, and many a mile of dense old forest. In short, it was a right royal demesne, and not an acre of it all had been shorn from the estate since the statute of Edward I. had put a stop to the increase of manors in the realm. _

It was towards noon of a pleasant day late in the summer that two men stood by the lodge-gate of Birchmear Park. One of them was Peter Brun, the keeper, and the other seemed a traveller, having a pack upon his back, and dust upon his homely garb. Both were men past the middle-age. "I declare, Peter, it does me good to see you— to see that you are so hale and so hearty. You have an easy time at the old place." "Those generally have easy times, Jason, that have a mind to make 'em easy. As for me, I take things as the come, and don't borrow trouble from what don't concern me. If I did 1 might find plenty of it." "That's true, Peter. If people would only take the trouble that they're obliged to take, and be content to make the best of it, there wouldn't be so much suffering as there is. I think I've bor- rowed trouble in my life that I didn't need." "And yet," said the lodge-keeper, with a measured shake of the head, "there be those upon whom trouble seems to come whether they will or not. It comes when they don't expect it, and when they don't deserve it." "Yes," responded Jason Smart, reflectively. "I've seen such ' • poor unfortunates, who were continually shouldering trials that came upon them as storms upon the traveller in the forest. But I hope you aren't one o' them, Peter." "No, no; not I, Jason; but I've seen it. But come; I've got something in the lodge that 11 do you more good than to stand here with your pack on your back. And I've got a spare bed, too, old fellow: so if you like to rest, be it a few hours or a few days, there's a chance for you." They went into the lodge together, and when the guest had removed his pack, and brushed the dust from his clothing, the keeper set out a pot of ale, with bread and cold meat; and straightway Jason Smart gave ample token of appreciation and grati- tude by his works. When he had eaten and drank he moved back from the table and filled his pipe, and when the tobacco had been lighted to his satisfaction he turned once more to his enter- tainer. "Now, Peter, I want you to tell me about the family. Let me see. It 's almost a score of years since I left Birchmear. Sir John was then hale and hearty, and full fifty years old; and we thought he would never marry, but I hear he has done it." " Yes," said the keeper, slowly, "he has done It twice—which was just once too much. But I'll tell you all about it, if you have a mind to listen." "Go on, Peter." The lodge-keeper refilled the ale-pot, and having taken a moderate draught, he commenced: "You remember that his lordship lived those many years a bachelor on account of a bitter disappointment in early life. He had made up his mind that he would never marry; but he found reason to change his purpose. Out in India there was a certain Tom Rainsford—a younger brother of one of Sir John's schoolmates—to whom his lordship was particularly attached. I think Sir John bought his first commission for him. But, be that as it may, he worked his way up into the higher commissions by his own bravery and devotion. This Tom Rainsford was a colonel, and _ _ . .

were likewise small, ana nis step was noiseless ana catlike. He wore a shooting-jacket of brown velvet, and his jewelry was abundant and of fine quality. His age might have been anywhere from five-and-thirty to forty, perhaps just half way between the two points. The woman was older, and though she bore some features in common with her companion, especially about the eyes and mouth, yet she was what the world might call handsome—that is hand- some for one who had passed the meridian of life. She, too, carried her embonpoint to the verge of fatness, though her carriage was graceful and her form not at all unseemly. The only marked disproportion was in the head. She lacked the broad base which characterised the head of her companion, so that the member was small—far too small for either beauty or symmetry. When dressed for company she could so arrange her coiffure as to hide in a measure this cranial deficiency; but now she was in her morning robes and her hair-dresser had not performed her daily task. Let it not be understood that the woman lacked brain. Far from it. But her head was not of the true female type. It lacked the domestic group of organs, being almost flat at the back where the head of the true woman swells so grandly. "What do you think of that woman ?" asked the keeper, after the twain had passed on. "I don't know about the woman—l aint a judge of the sex—but I should say the man was a villain. Who is he?" "Ho calls himself the Honourable Harold Berwick." "And the woman is his mother?" " Yes ; she is the present Lady Birchmear." "And can't you see by the looks of that man's face and by the way he whispers what he's got to say that he's concocting some sort of villainy ? " "If he isn't, he's out of his regular line." "I should say so. And sum don't look like a saint. See how eager she is. I tell you, Peter, if there's villainy afoot she's got as much interest in It as he has. Mark my words."

div.p: CHAPTER IT.

PLOTTING. When Lady Birchmear and her son had passed from sight, the keeper and his companion came out into the path and pursued their way towards the mansion. Before entering the court, Jason desired to visit the grounds beyond, so they passed round under the great oak trees that shaded the southern wing of the pile at a short distance from which point they found themselves in the garden. "There is the old summer-house and the foun- tain," cried the old-time servitor. "I declare, they look just as they did a score of years ago." "Things haven't changed much in that time," said the keeper. "Sir John takes a pride in pre- serving the old landmarks." "Hold on " internipted Jason; here comes another man in our way." " Where ?" _

" e.13-1:-:-c-o.ming out from the summer-house. "0 ! we needn't hide from that man. Yon shall know him, Jason; you shall say he is a gentleman worth knowing, too. That is our young master, Arthur." And thus speaking the ker,pPr led the way towards the summer-lion:3e, stopping u hen within a few yards of where the young man stood. And this was the son of Tom and Isabel Rains- ford, now called Arthur Berwick. He was a youth of three-and-twenty ;.tall and strong, and possess. lug a symmetry of form that ;mignt have served a sculptor for an Achilles or an Apollo. His hair, which ;was of a iwltrons golden hue, clung about his finely-shaped head in closely clustering ringlets, and one or two of be fugitive circlets that fell upon the broad and open brow served, by delicate contrast, to show bow pure and perfect was his skin. His face was haint,onte beyond a question. And it was more than handsome. Not only were the features beautifully moulded and turned, but they were illumined and warmed by a frank and generous uprising of spirit—a bold and manly truthfulness—and a clear beaming of the deep blue eyes that betokened a heart equally distant from guile and fear. As he moved along, at an easy, swinging pace, it was very plain to be seen that his physical system was in perfect tune, his muscles wondrously developed, and his vitality of the very highest order, both in quantity and quality. A close observer, and one skilled in detecting such things, might have discovered an unnatural flush upon the cheeks, and a lack of that perfect pearly lustre which belonged to eyes like his; and he might have discovered, too, that lines of care and unrest were being drawn upon his brow and about his finely-formed mouth. The young man wore a morning jacket of purple velvet, neatly trimmed with gold cord ; and his only ornament of jewelry was a bosom-pin, of gold, representing two female figures holding aloft a diamond of the first water, and of unusual size. This stone of inestimable value, had been pre- sented to dol. Tom Rainsford by a wealthy rajah whose life he had saved at Allahabad ; and Tom, when dying, had left it for his son. More than once, while at Oxford, when Arthur would have pledged his last change of raiment for money, had petty bankers offered to advance large sums upon the diamond; but he had held it as a part of his very life—as the only connecting link between himself and the memory of his dead father—and no amount of impecunious suffering had led him to think of parting with it, even for a time. "Peter, my old friend l" cried the youth, as he saw the keeper approaching. "I give you a good day, Mr. Arthur," returned Peter, with a warmth that betokened the mingling of love with respect. "I am taking the liberty, sir of showing an old friends over the grounds. This is Jasdn Smart, Who used to be a groom at Birchmear, a score of years ago." Arthur greeted Jason very kindly, and remarked that he had often heard of him.

"It was a grand old place in those years, your honour, and it is a grand old place yet," said Jason; "and I shouldn't have left, only his lord- ship hired a head-groom who was afraid of me. But that's neither here nor there. Sir John waa always a friend to me; or, leastwise, he meant to be." " Yonr experience is not a solitary one," remarked Arthur, with a smile. But the smile quickly faded away, and he added, half to himself; "The best of men may have evil influences brought to bear upon them. We don't always know when fortune may be smiling upon us through a mask." "Cod send that Dame Fortune may never smile falsely upon you, Mr. Arthur," ejaculated Peter, fervently. "[hank you, Peter. And I may add, that I fully 'lelieye, if your prayers could be an- swered, I should be a fortunate and a happy

"That you would, sir—that you would!" "And now, Peter, have you seen Harold in the park ? " "Yes, sir. I saw him, but a short time ago, on the other side—he and his mother walking together." "He and his mother 7" "Ye,, sir." "Chatting leisurely, I suppose?" "No, sir. Talking as though their very liven were at stake." . _

- A cloud came upon the young man's face and his hands were involuntarily clenched. Thekeeper marked the effect of his announcement, and presently said I " Arthur, if I can help you, you may command me. I can see what's going on, and I know that his lordship is being blinded—" " Rush, Peter I" interposed the youth, putting forth his hand. "I thank you kindly; and if want help I will not fear to tax you. But I hope I may not be in the need. My sojourn at Birch- mear will be not long extended.' "You will not—" "I hope to go into the army, my good Peter." "Sir John will got you a commission, then?"

• - "If he does not, I may get one for myself. But I am not gone yet." And with these words Arthur Bemick turned away. "Aye," he added to himself, when he was alone, "as a last chance I can pledge my father's diamond, and raise the price of the best commission to be bought. Fear not," he continued, raising his eyes as though speaking with a spirit that might hover near, " if I pledge it I will redeem it, if I live. If I am forced to part with this only ' token of thy love, my father, I will be a very miser until I can gain it back !" hat do you think of him ?" asked the keeper of his companion, after Arthur had left them. " What can any man think that's got eyes in his head and wit in his brain ?" returned Jason, enthusiastically. "I never saw a finer fellow. And it's plain to be seen that he s a man—every inch of him." "He'd make a grand soldier," suggested Peter. "Yes," admitted Jason; "but it would be the ap piling of a lord." " Zounds l you're right, old fellow. The country can't spare such men. Birchtnear needs him more than the army does; and Enzland needs him in the House of Lords. I

, nowt proiess to know mucn aoou sueri things, but I've got an idea that real, noble-hearted, true, whole-souled men aren't any too plenty up there where the peers of the realm sit." "But," added Jason, by way of compromise, "let come what will, that young man will make his mark, if he lives. If he joins the army, he'll make a solcier that England'll be proud of." "Aye, that's true," responded the keeper. They walked on a few paces, and then he continued: "I sometimes think, Jason, that things aint exactly as they should be in this world. Now look at these two men. Arthur has right on his side; and when it comes to the matter of strength, he could handle Harold as I would handle a child. And yet see how the case really stands. The jackal is likely to rout the lion." "That's the narrow vision of human eyes," said Jason, correctively. "The end is more than you or I can see." There was a grain of comfort in this which the keeper had not before discovered, and when he had considered it, he found it tangible. But they had now entered the summer-house, and their attention was called to other things. And now, while the two old servants are viewing familiar objects, we will follow Lady Birchmear and her son. They had entered upon a secluded spot, away from the principal paths, where they had stopped, and where they pursued the conversation in which they had been engaged—pursued it to a point upon which they had not ventured while in a more exposed part of the ground*. " "My mother," said Harold, in a voice scarcely , raised above a whisper, "what we do must be done quickly. It is very evident that Sir John still cherishes a lingering love for Arthur, in spite of his dissipations." "I think he does," asserted her son. "He cherishea for the bey an instinct of love above me, just as he remembers the boy's mother with a warmer feeling than he bestows upon my mother." Lady Birchmear clutched her hands, and breathed quickly: "You need not mention that, Harold. I know his lordship's heart, and he may bestow its treasures of empty remembrance where he will, so that I bend his outward acts to my purpose. In all things but this he is my abject slave." "I know," said Harold, with an evil smile, "that you have entire control of all that can affect your individual interests, and now It only remains for us to gain control of the rest. Shall we let Arthur gain a commission in the army ?" "No 1" answered the lady, emphatically, "You, my son, must be heir of Birchmear and that you may never be if Arthur leaves us and enters the army." "You speak as though you had full assurance, nay mother." "Aye, Harold, and I have full assurance. I knew Arthur's father, and had he lived one poor month longer he would have been a general of brigade. His son is like him. Let Arthur go out to India with a commission and he will make a record of which Sir John will be proud. The old man's slumbering love will be rekindled, and we shall find him watching the Gazette with a pleasure that will entirely obliterate the memory of the ill- reports from Oxford." "I understand you," said the son, with an un- comfortable look upon his face. He could not deny the premises, and yet it was cutting to be brought thus face to face with his youthful rival's excellencies. "And, furthermore," pursued her ladyship, "I can read in Arthur's frank and open front that he will turn over a new leaf if he can get away from Birchmear with honour. Mind you, I am calling things now by their right names; you and I can- not deceive each other. I can see that your rival wants to regain the ground he has lost, and I can see also that as he grows older he gathers more manly and sober inspirations." Harold smiled incredulously. "It is even so, my son; and if you will be frank you will find yourself forced to confess that you have hard work to urge him into debauch." "Egad, my lady, you are right, and if I had not your assistance I might often fail in the work." Her ladyship did not wince at this. She acknow- ledged the recognition of her services by anod, and then went on: "I have undertaken a work, and I shall not shrink from any ordinary means necessary to its ae:complishment. You know that I have sought to poison his lordship's mind against the youth, and I have so far succeeded that if we can bring about some emphatic development—something that shall fall crushingly upon him—we may get him out of the way. And this you must do. You know how anything like contention or open strife jars upon Sir John's nerves. Now can you not fasten a quarrel upon Arthur? I think his peculiar temper- ament is more open to that means of attack than to any other. Mark me: If this youth inherits Birch in ear—' "He shall never do it ! " interrupted Harold, with an oath. "I have set my heart upon the prize and I will win it, or, at all events, the son of the first wife shall not win it from me. You spoke of engaging him in a quarrel. By the mass! You have opened the way to a new mine. A plan already begins to shape itself in my mind. Let me think.

..... He walked away by himself, and when he returned there was a new look of hope upon his evil face. "My mother, I think I have it. I am well acquainted with several of the officers of the—the Regiment, at present quartered at Saudsport. The major and two of the captain's have been chums of mine in India; and among the subalterns is a young lieutenant who is beholden to me for an important service. You have heard me speak of Liouel Talford ?" "The young officer whom you extricated from the hands of the police at York ?" "The very same. He is a light-headed, rollicking fellow, and I know would do me a good turn. I must bring him over here. Will you break the Ice of Sir John's reserve, and open the way for the reception of a few of these officers? By the way— the old major is a friend of his lordship's." "I will join you, Harold." "All right ; and when the thing is settled I will ride over to Saudsport with the invitations. If Talford does not fail me, we'll spring a mine upon Master Arthur"that shall send him flying." "But be careful, my son. All may depend upon your care and circumspection. While Sir John suspects nothing of this I can lead him ; but let him gain but an inkling of a suspicion that you and I were aiming at this peerage of Birchmear, and I think your last hope would be gone. Understand, Harold, what we both have at stake. You have the most. Let Sir John die when he will, I, if I outlive him, shall be still Lady Birch- wear." " until a new Lacy Btrentnear sets you down as Dowager," suggested Harold, with a smile. "That I must fApect in time," returned her ladyship; "but when I become Dowager Lady Birchmear I only ask that my own son's wife may take my place at the head of the amily." "la which event I have a decided interest," added the gentleman. • "And to which end," suggested the lady, "you must work diligently. But we must remain here no longer. I will see you again this evening." It was not until after dinner, when his lordship had suffered himself to be persuaded into breaking an extra bottle of wine, that . Lady Birchmear ventured to approach him upon the subject of a party. She thought it would relieve the monotony of life at the manor; and she ventured to hope that the occasion might serve to entertain himself. There were a number of the neighbouring families whom she would like to call in; and Harold had Intimated that he would like to invite Alajor Thorpe, with one or two other offices, from Saudsport. "Bless me ! " cried Sir John. "I remember Major Thorpe very well. He was on my staff at Calcutta. I'should like to see him by all means. He and I can sit over our wine while you younger ones find sport in the park." "For sham ! Sir John," said Lady Birchmear, tapping him upon the shoulder with her fan. " You mean that as a slur." "A slur ? " repeated the baron, in surprise. "Aye, a slur upon me, because you think I have not reached that respectable age to which you your- self have attained., " Respectable age! Why, bless my soul, I'm an old man—an old, old man ! ' "My dear Sir John, you will drive me to say something etisagiceable by and by. It is not the accumulation of years that makes a man old. In health, and strength, and vigour, and intellectual altivity, there is perpetual youth; and allow me to ask you if you fail in any of these ? And, having asked the question, allow me to answer it. Why do I love you, and honour you, and lean upon you? 0, fie I Sir John. You will be taunting me with my age next. We have both been younger, I know; but let us hold our hearts above the touch ot the frost

Professor Huxley voted at least once in a muni- cipal election at Eastbourne, but he was not so in- terested in local politics as he was in one or two of the philanthropic institutions of Eastbourne. The Professor was rarely seen in the town, but might, until his illness, have been constantly met on the breezy downs of Heachy Head. Like Mr. Gladstone, he would often walk holding his hat in his hand. He had in early life considerable knowledge of the poverty-stricken side of London. One of his remarks on this theme is worth recalling. "On a I voyage round the world I had opportunity of see- ing savage life in all conceivable conditions of de- gradation, and in this experience of mine I found nothing more degrading, nothing so hopeless, nothing nearly so intolerably dull and miserable, as the life I had left behind in the East of London. If the alternative were presented to me to choose the life of one of these people in the East-end or that of a savage, I would distinctly choose the latter."

The" Athenmum " announces that Messrs. Smith, Elder. and Co., have paid " well over a thousand pounds for Mrs. Humphrey Ward's new novel " The Story of Bessie Costrell." As the work is quite a short one, consisting a some two thousand nine hundred and forty lines—ten words to the line—it is to be reckoned that Mrs. Ward has ob- tained nearly seven shillings for every line, and something like ninepence for every word. This is excellent pay,rarely exceeded by anything previous writers have received. There are, however, cases in which authors have got a good deal more.

More news of the substantial results of the popu- larity gained by English actors in America. Mr. Dominick Murray, a favourite London comedian fully thirty years ago, has been ever since equally popular in the United State', with the result that he is about to retire with a fortune of thirty thousand pounds. He has invested the greater part of this money in a magnificent estate in Canada—perhaps with a lingering desire to spend his remaining years beneath the British flag—and he will settle down in his new bomo at the close of his present engagement in " The Cotton King."

Mr. Jesse Collings has given a foretaste on the Standing Committee on Trade of his powers as a constructive statesman. True, he confined himself to one or two points, for more important matters appear to have claimed his attention until the pro- ceedings were drawing to a clo.e. But Mr. Col- lings's capacity for fussy and futile talk, for ped- dling views of things, and for the temper best described as that of the scold, came out strongly when he posed as the champion of the distressed washerwoman. Her right to work day and night without any sanitary or ihdustrial protection was insisted upon by the new Secretary. The washer- woman represented, in his mind, the interests of the small industry, the small occupier, the little man "on the make." Those are the interests, those are the persons, for whom Mr. Chamberlain's new clerk of the works is to turn on, or perhaps WA should say switch off, the machinery of the State. We shall look with interest for the new experi- ments in contracting out at the Home Office. It was Mr. Collings who, alone amongst the members on the Grand Committee, declared that the Factory Bill would never pass. Well, it is going to pas, I but what will Mr. Collings do with it?

• No one quite likes the interposition of a general election just now. The banks like It least. of all, because it very much interferes with their quiet and ordinary methods of doing businesq. The Wrowing improvement in certain branches in Lon- don has been stopped. and wholesale houses com- plain that few orders are cruninz in from the coun- try, whilst. foreign orders have begun to decline much earlier in the summer than usual. "It is cuttin,, short onr summer season in every way," it, the an- mer given to one of my inquiries. "It means. also, an early winter seasmn: Provincial traders kre saying very much the same. Happily all will be over promptly.

div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

The Felect Committee presided over by Sir Henry Roscoe, M.P. on Monday agreed upon a report strongly recommending the legalising of the use of the metrical aN stem of weights and measures and vital that system should be compulsorily alopted after a period of two years.

I cannot believe that there is any truth in the story that the resignation of the Bake of Cam- bridge is to be withdrawn. The Duke of Devon- shire is a man of consistency ; and although he was not very active in pressing forward the reforms which his Commission recommended, it is incred- ible that he would consent to a reversal of the much-needed and long-delayed steps which the late Governmentlad just resolved upon when they came to grill. The fact, however, that Sir H. Campbell-Bannerman was censured immediately after announcing the Government scheme, and some other curieus incidents which have occurred in connection with the War Office, have given colour to the sensational reports which are all git in regard to the administration of this department, and there is considerable anxiety among army re- formers lest a great " job " of some sort should be in prospect. It is perfectly certain that the ob- structive set at the War Office will heartily welcome the change of Ministry, even :hough in the.enelitmay prove that c.hey gain nothing by it

1 •Surprise has been expressed in some ,quarters that Lord Salisbury has retained Lord Cross in his Cabinet while di:Tensing with the services of younger and more sp-to-date politicians. The ex- rlanation is, no doubt, that Lord Cross was in- cluded at her SI ajesty's,special request. tie is one of the' Queen's executors, he transacts a good deal of her confidential business for her, and is honoured with her entire personal confidence. Ender these circumstances it is easily to he understood that the 'Queen desireshim to remain in the responsible posi- tion of Cabinet Minister.

'Lord Salisbury's difficulties with his former col- leagues, whom he has been competed by the exi- gencies of Coalition to leave out in the cold, began after he had appointed their successors ; and he 'felt obliged in courtesy to inform them of the rea- •sons for his neglect. To this end he has written a series of letters which we hear described as being of the most graceful, affectionate, and ever touching ,character. In fact, the letter forwarded by Lord Salisbury to Lord Inutsford ha, it is said, brought tears, not only to the eyes of its recipient, but to other people who have been permitted to read it.

Mr. Chamberlain, in his address to the electors of West Birmingham, says :—" The new Governir ent recognises their primary duty,* t&c. In this passage the word "Government," it will be noticed, has in agreement with it a verb in the singular,and imme- diately thereafter a pronoun in the plural. It is a small matter, of course, hut it seems piquantly characteristic of a gentleman who is changeable in his moods.

The Rev. Benjamin Waugh has retired from the editorship of the "Sunday Magazine," his work in connection with.the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children leaving him no leisure for other labours. Mr. William Canton will conduct the magazine.

The references in the newspapers of the late Pro Huxley's career se a rule touch only lightly on that side of his life which a man cares not to lay bare to the world. But those who knew him well will call to mind how he loved to pay tireless tribute to the influence wrought upon his life work by the wife tor whom he had waited well nigh as long as Jacob waited for Rachel. He reaped the reward of that patience in a union of forty years, unclouded save by such shadows as bereavement casts. They were as lovers to the end. The heaviest loss that befel the home was in the death of the gifted daughter, who, true artist herself, had married the lion. John Collier. While scarcely out of her teens her picture of a group of children play- ing cards in a garret, entitled, " The Sins of their Fathers," was exhibited in the Royal Academy. Even in the subject thus chosen there was evident the influence of home teaching on the doctrine of heredity ! We have reason to know that the father felt more vanity over that work than anything ever done by him had inspired.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 6 1895.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 6 1895.
WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the Council was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Councillor James Fairdough) presided,and there were aTtio present Aldermen Grsenall, Blackhurst, Sutton, Fiancomb ; Councillors Roberts, Shaw Green, Cannell, Hill, Shill- cock, Langton, Lee, Evans, Bennett, Skelton, Woods, Garner, Wilkinson, Baird., Plumpton, Monks, Heaton, Elepherd, Greening, Shaw ; Messrs. Whittle (town clerk), Fairhurst (borough treasurer), Longdin (borough surveyor).

, WATCH COMMITTEE : THE MINE GING ORDER. kt a meeting of the above committee it was resolved that the Town Clerk give notice requiring preper muzzles to be used " so as to prevent dogs from inflict- ing injury with their teeth to any person or any dog or other animal." The minutes were confirmed on the motion of the Maros, seconded by Alderman Serrom FINANCE AND ESTATE COMMITTEE. In moving the confirmation of the minutes of this committee, Counoillor SHAW GREEN said the Council would be pleased to know that the committee were having no difficulty in replacing the bonds withdrawn owing to the reduction of the rate of interest. Councillor BENNETT referring to the favourable report of the borough auditors as to the books and accounts of the Corporation,said that whilst the accounts of the Cor- poration were being placed on a very good footing, and every praise was due to Mr. Fairhurst, he was still of opinion that they would not be vite satisfactory until they bad had a municipal balance sheet representing the assets and liabilities of the Corporation. There were I ' difficulties about the preparation of such a sheet, but they had been overcome in other instances. Their ac- counts were anomalous and incomplete until they had an account by which they could show that their in- debtedness amounted to over half-a-million, and that they had Assets which amounted to nearly the same sum. Councillor SHAW-GREEN said that was a matter which had been under consideration some time. A vast am- ount Ofltime would be required to complete the work suggested, and the enormous growth of work in the de- partment made it difficult to deal with it. At the same time the subject was receiving the attention of the Com- mittee.

The minutes were then agreed to. THE HEALTH COMMITTEE.—TWO LOCAL NUISANCES. Alderman SUTTON moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Health Committee. Councillor R. T. Fars:motion asked if steps were being , taken to improve the condition of the old river at Wil- derspool ? The health of the inhabitants was suffering lin consequence of the condition of that river, and he thought the Corporation ought to enforce their views by deputation or otherwise upon the Rivers Pollution Com- mittee. (Hear,hear.) 'Councillor WOODS referred to the same subject, and pointed out that no fewer than 12 or 14 houses on the Wilderspool Causeway were vacant this week owing to the abominable stench from the river, which was injuri- ous to the health of the inhabitants. (Hear,hear.) Councillor PLUMPTON contended that Sankey Brook was in S worse condition than the river. The stench from the brook was " something fearful," and people living half-a•mile away were complaining about it. Councillor MONKS supported Councillor Plumpton's remarks as to Sankey Brook which, he said, was a much older nuisance than that at Wilderspool. Be thought that if they had two or three Aldermen living at Bank Quay, much more would have been heard of Sankey Brook dur- ing the past seven years. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were confirmed.
PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.-SETTS FOR BRIDGE
STREET.

This Committee recommended that the remaining por- tion of Bridge-st. be paved with setts, and that estimates and tenders be obtained for the construction of a wharf in front of Howley store yard. Councillor HEATON proposed the adoption of the miuutes and Councillor R. T. Ktiectouom seconded. The DEPUTY-MAYOR asked Councillor Heaton if it were not possible to pave the portion of Bridge-st, with wood instead of with setts. Councillor Haim&Ts supported, saying that the noise occasioned by Bo much traffic over the setts was almost intolerable in so narrow a street. It was said that the gradient of the thoroughfare was too great for it to be paved with wood, but he knew that there w, re streets paved with wood which were much steeper. Councillor HEATON, in reply, said the committee had paved one portion of the street with setts, and he might say that they had not received the slightest complaint of noise, but that the property owners were more pleased with these setts than they were with macadam. The minutes were approved. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

From the rep-or-t of Inspector to the Committee it ap- peared that 18 cases had been taken before the Magis- trates and -fines inflicted in 16 cases 1 hoy sent to the " Clio," and 1 warrant ordered ; 20 cases were brought before the Committee and dealt with ; that the Town Hall, Park and Baths Committee be requested to make make provision in Bank House at an early date for the accommodation of this department. The adoption of the minutes was moved by Councillor &taw -GREEN, seconded by Councillor SuicLcoca. ' In reply to questions Councillor Dr. CANNELL stated that the Town Hal, &cc., Committee proposed to spend £25 on the conversion of Bank House, which sum would make the place very comfortable for the requirements of the committee.
. .... _ The minutes were passed unanimously. MUSEUM, &C., COMMITTEE.

. . The Museum Committee report the following gifts : Two stone celts, and fossils, from Ballintoy, County Antrim ; birds' eggs (30) from Rathlin Island, from Mr. Longdin ; Tanager, Pyzranga rubra, from Mr. T. G. Carter ; wasp's nest, from Thelwall, from M-ijor Pick- mere ; nest and eggs of blackcap, from Aston-by-Sutton from Mr. H. Hobrts ; " Work of the Holy Spirit," by Lowry ; Parliamentary papers (28 parts), from Mr. R. Pierpoint ; " proceedings of Warringt u Literary and Philosophical Society," 1894-5, from the Society ; " Pro- ceedings of Warrington LIIPIRIV and, Philosophical Society," 1894-5, from Mr. F. W. Monks. The minutes were approved on the proposition of Councillor ROBERTS, seconded by Councillor GREENING.

div.head: CEMETERY COMMITTEE.
div.p: CEMETERY COMMITTEE.

From the report of the Registrar of this Committee it appeared that the interments for the past four weeks were—adults 49 ; minors; 32; stillborn and premature 5, Corresponding period last vear—adults, 40 ; minors, 55 ; stillborn and premature, 16. The receipts for the past four weEks were £95 Bs. 11d. ; corresponding period last year, £95 17s. 3d. Councillor RILL proposed the confirmation of the minutes, and observed that the cnnonttee were endea- vouring to improve the appearance of the cemetery as much as they could. Councillor BAIRD seconded, and the minutes were carried.
TOWN ALL, PARK, AND BATHS COMMITTEE:

The report of the batlikeeper shows that the income from the baths For the past two weeks was £5O 17s. 61., and for the corresponding period last year £26 I.ls. 61; increase, £24 65. The total income of the Markets Committee from all sources for the past five weeks WAS £406 I.oi. 7d.; cor- responding period last year, £390 12s. 31. ; increase, £l5 Be. 4d. . .
Councillor Dr. CARRELL proposed the approval of the minutes, and *drew attention to the satisfactory increase in the receipts of the bathe. The DEPUTY-MAYOR seconded. _

&IN:16110r GREENING thought it would be advisablelo place a few mere seats in the Park. Such an increase of accommodation would be very much valued by the ratepayers. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR said that more seats were in process of erection. The minutes were accepted. MARKET 3 COMMITTEE.
The minutes of this committee were passed. on the motion of Alderman GREENALL, seconded by Alderman BLACICHU
RIVERS COMMITTEE-LIVELT DISCUSSIONS.

The minutes of this ceinmittee which we published last week, and which were identical with those referred back to the committee at the previous Council meeting, were moved by Councillor ROBERTS. During the course of his remarks Councillor ROBERTS said that he need not refer to the fact that at the last meeting ot the Council the two important minutes again submitted were not confirmed. Since then the Rivers Committee had met and had given every possible con- sideration to the recommendations whiJh they now sub- mitted to the Council. So far as the first was concerned the committee, with one exception, unanimously confirmed their previous recommendation. In re2ard to the recommendation to let a plot of land to Messrs. Bishop and Co. for a wharf, he was sorry to have to refer to a matter which was somewhat personal. He had been informed that a statement had been circulated to the effect that certain members of the committee and himself were interested in a certain com- pany which had been recently form-d and that that company had a direct interest in procuring a lease of the wharf, and that certain members of the Council, very properly believing that the committee had no right to usurp their positions as members of the Corporation for anything that might seem to favour a personal interest, voted against the proposition. He was extremely sorry that any member of the Council should think it possible that any member of the Rivera Committee would he a party to such conduct, If the slightest pQssible inquiry had been made into the facts of the case it would have been seen at once that no such interest wig held by any , member of the committee. For himself he could say that neithrr on that oca Asian, nor on any previous occa- sion, nor as long as he retline,l a seat in the Corporation would hein the slichest decree aqempt to uso his posi- tion for his own personal advantage, or the advantage of anyone with whom he might be connected. No mom- her of the committee had the slightest interest in bring- ing the matter forward except for the benefit of War- rington as a whole. They had no personal intere t in the matter to the extent of a single sixpence. This s'atement would probably enable some members of the Council to reconsider their decision. There had only two objections been made to the proposal of the Committee. The first one was that by the le' ting oh this wharf they would enable competition—unfair competition—to be

set up with the Manchester Ship Clonal Company. He had only to remind the Council that the Manchester Ship Canal Company had given their consent and had particularly expressed their approval of the wharf, so that they, at any rate, were not afraid of this competi- tion. In addition to that, the gentleman who repre- sented Messrs. Bishop and Company attended the meet- ing of the Rivers Committee and told the members dis- tinctly that their object in securing this wharf was that of bringing their mat.. rials to and from their works on 1 the lea t expsnsive plan possible. It was possible that in addition to that, they might do some slight amount of public carrying but it could not possibly be to that ex- tent as to damage the Manchester Ship Canal Company. and he(Councillor Roberts)was of the opinion that It WRS the duty of the Council, so far as it could, to offer facili- ties to every manufacturer in Warrington who was a ratepayer, because by doing so they would help to estab- lish industries in the town, and therefore increase the rateable value. The firm in question had brought a new industry into the town and were anxious to develop it, and the Council, as the custodians of the public inter- ests and rights, were well within their duty in offering every facility which did not injure the ratepayers gener- ally to a firm of this aharacter to improve their posi- tion. Objection had been made that this charge of 2d. per ton to the Corporation would not be fair, but they had that night had submitted to them by the Paving and Sewerage Committee a proposal to obtain estimates for the construction of a wharf a little higher up at the Corporation storeyard, so that that disposed of any argument that there was any risk in letting that wharf, as the Corporation were going to erect a wharf of their own for dealing with their own material at the earliest possible date, and in his opinion very properly PO too. On behalf of Messrs. Bishop and Co., he might say that it was particularly through their intervention they as a Corporation had become possessed of this foreshore and they were going to receive a rent of £2O a year, if the Council sanctioned the proposal, for what previously I brought them in nothing. They had become the owners 'of the foreshore in addition to that, with all the rights appertaining thsreto, and the terms of the proposed tenancy were in every way favourable to the Corpora- tion. Be therefore hoped the Council would see its way to the letting of the wharf. With regard to the proposal that the Chairman be ap- pointed to represent the Corporation on the Upper Mer- sey Navigation Corn mission for the term of three years, Councillor Roberts said there was no desire on the part of the Committee to be harsh with Councillor Richard Fairclough. The committee asked the Council to believe that they were anxious to obtain the best value for the appointment they could obtain. The Standing Orders gave the Rivers Committee great power as would be seen from the following extract :—One of the duties of the Committee was " To enforce and carry out the provi- sions of the Rivers Pollution Prevention Acts, 1876 and 1893, or of any other general or local Act with respect to matters relating to the navigation and improvement of the river, and to the prevention of floods. And the said committee shall have, and this Council hereby dele- gate to the said committee, all and every the powers, authorities, and discretion which by the said Acts in relation to the matters and purposes aforesaid are now given to and vested in this Council." Without wishing to be in the slightest degree disrespectful to the Council, he contended that the Council had given away to the Rivers t,ommittee all the power which they ever pos- sessed in regard to the nomination and appointment of a Commissioner, and he proceeded to endeavour to show that the committee had precedents in their favour for the steps they were now taking. The first Commissioner, the late Alderman Joseph Davies, was appointed in 1876 Prior to the appointment of the Rivers' Committee. In 1879 the committee was appointed, and tie continued to be the Commissioner as tong as he remained chairman of the committee. Councillor R. T. Fairtmotion : Mr. Crosfield was Chairman of the Committee. Councillor WOODS said Cabncillor Davies had said that his father was not Chairman of the Committee. Councillor ROBERTS said Alderman Davies was chair- man of the Rivers Committee when he was put upon it. Councillor Fairclough succeeded to the chairmanship when Alderman Davies retired and he (Mr. Roberts) succeeded Mr. Fairclough. He was not speaking about what he did not know. He was not saying that Mr. Davies was chairman of the committee from the first, but he was up to the time this change was made in the appointment of commissioner. Councillor Roberts re- lated the circumstances under which the change was made, and said that it was in February, 1892, that the Council adopted a recommendation of the Rivers Com- mittee that the chairman of the Rivers Committee (not Councillor Richard Fairclough) be appointed to repre- sent the Corporation on the Upper Mersey Navigation Commission for the term of three years. Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH said that whenever the Chairman of a Committee was appointed to anything the Town Clerk always put the "Chairman of the Com- mittee" and did not name him on the minutes. If the Mayor was appointed to an office, the Town Clerk did not say Councillor Fairclough but" the Mayor," and the same with the Chairman of a Committee. He gave this explanation at the last meeting. Councillor ROBERTS said he remembered very well the diacussion which took place and the conclusion the com- mittee came to, and that was the same conclusion they had since come to, that the Chairman of the committee for the time being should be the representative on this commission. He had said he thought they had the law on their WE., he had proved conclusively that they had precedent on their side, and he ventured to suggest that they had also commonsense on their side. (Laughter ) It was all a matter of opinion, of course. Without wish- ing to be in the slightest degree offensive to Councillor Fairclough or anybody else, he thought the present chairman of the Rivers Committee was quite as compe- tent as any other member of the Council to adequately represent the interests of Warrington even upon the Upper Mersey Navigation Commission. (Laughter.) It was simply his own opinion : others might not hold it. (Hear, hear.) But he did ask, not as a personal matter, for that did not weigh with him, but in the face of the fact that the committee had given their most serious consideration to these two important matter., they would not without very good reason indeed practically assert their want of confidence in the committee by re- fusing to sanction the passing of the minute.. Councillor HEATON seconded the adoption of the minutes.

... _ HEPHERD said that for the third time, and he hoped for the last time, he had to propose an amend- ment with regard to the wharf let to Messrs. Bishop and Co., and it was that the minute of the committee relat- ing to it be net confirmed. He was very much astonished to find on Monday morning when he received the Council summons that the terms had been again put an the minutes. It seemed absurd that such a thing could be done, and he thought some rule should be made to pre- vent coin miteees bringing matters up time after time,at all events for a period of one or two years. Alderman GREENALL seconded the amendment.

Councillor PLUMPTON said he was under the impression at the last Council meeting that if the Corporation let the wharf they would be doing an injustice to them- selves,but since then he had found the Corporation were going to have a wharf of their own. There had been a letter in the papers from Messrs. Bishop and Co. from which it appeared that they had been promised this wharf if they got permission from certain authorities, and that permission they had got. He considered they were morally bound to let Messrs. Bishop and Co have the wharf if it was done without disadvantage to the Corporation. (Hear, hear.) He did not think there was any disadvantage to the Corporation, in fact, he thought they would be losing £2O a year, if they did not let it to the Cempany. The Corporation had safeguarded themselves in every way, and could take the wharf over any time they liked, if the Company did not act, fairly in the matter. He would support the minutes of the Committee.

Councillor R. T. FIaRCLOUGH said he did not f know whether many members hal been down to look at the proposed wharf. It was only 18 feet wide' and when they had taken 8 feet off that for a footpath he should be sorry for the wharf. He asked if the Committee were go- ing to let off the street as well as th footpath It was not a fit and proper place to make a wharf, because it would be so disadvantageous to the public, who wOuld have no free space to get to the river. It was the only little bit of land now by which they could get to the river. _ .

Alderman Sorrow said the terms upon which the Cor- poration were asked to let this piece of land•appeared to him very reasonable, and apart from any other consider- ation he did not think they could hesitate to let it. But whilst they might desire to encourage and assist every manufacturer and trade in the town, they must not en- deavour to do it to the detriment and at the expense of the community generally. As they all knew. the Man- chester Ship Canal Company were under an obligation to provide certain dock accommodation xvi'Aiin a specified time, and unless some definite arrangement was arrived at with regard to the use of the old river and the Ship Canal Company and the provision of dorks and wharves they might be doing an injustice net only to themselves and the general public hut to the Shiri !Canal Company. Unless these arrangements were finally settled with the Ship Canal Company, he thought it would be bettAr to defer the letting of this land. When Alderman Sutton sat down Councillors Woods, Longton. and Monks, rose to speak at the same time, but the Mayor called upon Councillor Monks to speak first Councillor Woods remained standing, apparantly dissatisfied at the Mayor's decision. The MAYOR, addressing Councillor Woods, said, " Don't glare at me in that manner." Couneillnr WOODS: I rose before. The MAYOR COMICMOT Monks rose before you, sir. I can See your expression from here. lam here to see fair play, at:d I am going to see it. Unineillor MONKS said he could not tell how surprised he was. as well as annoyed, that his name should hare been coupled with the company whizh had been recently formed. fie knew nothing whatever about the corn- Play beyond what tad appeared in the public papers a few weeks ago. HP was not a shareholder in the cora- tiany, nor had he even ben asked to take any shams in it,so that he could fairly la v claim to discuss this %natter in an entirely unprejudiced manner. (Hear, hear.) There was a much more important side of the question, and it was this : It was well-known that up to the present time, practically only the large manufacturers had been able to get any benefit out of the river.
It was those who had works on the. river bank,

and whe had ample means of providing them- selves with all the facilities requisite to enable them to get a full benefit of the cheap water transit. On the other band there werethe shopkeepers and small traders of the town,who in his opinion required as much if not more consideration at the hands of that Council than the large manufacturers to whom he had referred, who were perfectly well able to take care of themselves. These small traders from the very nature of circum- stances had been compelled to send away and receive all their goods either by the railway or the Ship Canal, all the owners of which acted in concert and worked under Conference arrangements, under which they made these traders pay the maximum tolls which their Acts of Par- liament allowed. These traders, who formed a large proportion of the population of Warrington, had thus been suffering under this disadvantage, while larger manufacturers bad been making the fullest use of the river. When a respectable firm like Bishop and Co. came forward with a proposal like the present one, though at present it was admittedly for their own business but which promised further develcpment by which these small traders and shopkeepers would have opportunities and facilities put in their way such as they 'never had before in the history of the town, it seemed to him that the proposal demanded the most favourable considera- tion not only of the Rivers' Committee but of the whole of the members of the Council. (Hear, hear.) The Riven,' Committee had spent a great deal of time over this subject, and as the result they had this proposed agreement which the Council at the last meeting con- sidered and in his opinion rejected without rhyme or reason. Was it to be wondered at that intelligent rate- payers should give credence to certain reports which had been freely circulated in the town that the business of the Council was all settled beforehand in the bar parlours of public-houses and at political clubs? (Coun- cillor Woons : " Nonsense.") Councillor Mortics said he felt that to some extent his reputation was at stake over this matter, because there was no doubt that members were influenced by the rumours that certain members of the Rivers' Committee would benefit by the proposed arrangement with Messrs. Bishop and Co., and his name was mentioned with others. Since he had been a member of the Town Coun- cil he had not given a single vote, nor said a single word, that was in any way likely to benefit himself or the con- cern with which he was connected, and aslong as he was in the Council he should take good care that no vote of his was influenced by considerations of that sort. (Hear, hear.) Councillor LONGTON said he had made careful inquiries since the last meeting of the Council, and he had not heard anything to show why the land should not be let for the purpose named to Messrs. Bishop and Co. It seemed to him that this was a trivial and a ridiculous opposition to Messrs. Bishop and Co. Councillor Wows was then called upon by the Mayor, and he responded with the words "Thank you." The MAYOR: You have no need to thank me,Councillor Woods, I am only doing what is right. Councillor Woos in the course of his speech strongly deprecated the remarks which Councillor Monks had made with regard to taprooms and political clubs. He contended that the Councillor had no right to make such a charge against a body of Councillors. As a gentleman he ought to withdraw the observatiun. He would not dare to make such a remark in an ordinary assembly of Englishmen if they were free and without a Chairman. Be would have to retract it.

Councillor &Law GREEN explained that he was the secretary of the company to which reference had been made, and it had been formed to conduct and manage some ships that would go to sea and could not possibly get to the wharf and have any connection with it in any way. He protested against any such suspicion influ- encing the Council. Councillor BENNETT denied that there would be an unfair competition with the Ship Canal Company by the letting of the wharf. It was childish to say that that would be the case. The Ship C.nal Company had not treated the Corporation with such magnanimity that the latter should consider them in the matter. At the pre- sent moment they had absolutely no benefit from the Canal.

- - Councillor ROBERTS said that Councillor Hepherd had given no reason for moving his amendment. Let the Council disestablish and disendow their minds once and for all of the fear that the Canal Company were not able to take care of themselves. The committee had to con- sider the interests of the people of Warrington, and not the interests of the Canal Campany. The voting was then proceeded with and for the amend- ment there voted :—The Mayor, Aldermen Greenall, Sutton, Francomb, and Blackhurst ; Councillors R. T. Fairclough, Dr. Cannel!, Hill, Lee, Evans, Woods,Shaw, Garner, Wilkinson, Baird, and Hepherd.-16. Against :—CounciUors Roberts,Green, Shillcock,Long- ton, Bennett, Skelton, Greening, Plumpton, Monks and Heaton.-10. The amendment was declared carried. Councillor HEPHERD then moved a further amendment that the resolutions relating to the appointment of a re- presentative on the Upper Mersey Navigation Commis- sion be not confirmed. He thought that as the Rivers' Committee had again brought the resolution before the Council after it had once been rejected it would be bet- ter to refer the matter to the General Purposes Com- mittee and let them appoint a representative. Alderman GREENALL seconded the amendment.

Councillor FAIRCLOUGEI said he was the person who first had the idea of having steamers on the river. He also mentioned various duties of the tipper Mersey Nevi- gation Commission. He contended that he must be the most suitable person to represent the Corporation on the Commission because their boats were constantly patrolling the river, whereas Councillor Roberts had no boats, and kmew nothing shout the buoys. Councillor Ronanrs : Who has no boats? Councillor FAIRCLOLIGH : You have not.

COUnalOr ROBERTS: I am a boat owner just as much as you are personally. I will tell you that. That shovis you know nothing about the matter. Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGII: Recently. Councillor ROBERTS : I have been a boat owner for seven years. and what you have just stated shows your ignorance of the facts. Councillor GREENING thought the discussion was out of order. but

The MAYOR said that the Town Clerk had told him that Councillor R. T. Fairclough was perfectly in order. Councillor R.T. FAX RCLOUGH said he had meant to say that he was in touch constantly with those who navi- gated the river. He felt in the position perhaps, for in- stance,of a governor of the Grammar School,who might not be re-appointed on the expiration of his term of office, although willing to continue his services. Would not any of the councillors think, if they were treated like this, that they had been slighted P It was a great slight on the part of the Rivers' Committee, to do what they were attempting to do at the present time. If he was not fit to retain his post, then he was not fit to re- tain his .positian on the Council.

Councillor ROBERTS said there was not the slightest idea in the minds of the committee of questioning Coun- cillor Richard Fairclough's fitness for the position. They all admitted there was no member of the Council who WAS better fitted to fill the position than Councillor Fair. dough. But that was not the point. The point was this : the Rivers' Committee was the only committee of the Corporation responsible for the management of the river, even including buoying and lighting. Every- thing which the Council had to do with regard to the river devolved upon the Rivers' Committee. Personally, he (Councillor Roberts) did not want the appointment, but on the contrary had pressed upon the committee to appoint Councillor Monks. That night, however, he argued, and very strongly too, that the man who was fit to be the chairman of the Rivers'Committee was quite as fit to represent the Corporation upon the Upper Mersey Navigation Commission. The discussion was continued by Alderman Sutton and Councilloz Longtoc. and the Council then divided when the following was the result :—For the amendment —Aldermen Greenall and Francomb : Councillors Dr. Cannel!. Hill, Shillcock, Loneton, Lee, Evans, Woods, Shaw, Baird and Flopherd7l2, . _

_ . Against—Alderman Sutton,Councillors Roberts,Green, Bennett, Wilkinson, Plumpton, Heaton, Green and Monks-9. The minutes as amended were then passed. FIRE ENGINE COMMITTEE. Councillor llHarms propo.ed the confirmation of the minutes which were published last week and Coun- cillar seconded. Councillor SHAW GREEN said that at the last meeting of the Council it was decided that a committee should be anpointed to consid.r the whole matter of improving the fire brigade. It witild be better, he thought, if the proposal to augment the brigade by six members was deferred until the Council was informed of what the newly-a ppointed committee intended doing. The MAYOR explained that the committee which it was decided to elect at the last Council meeting would be appointed that night. Councillor SKELTON proposed an amendment that the minutes referring to the proposal to atigmect the brigade he not passed. He agreed with the previous speaker that it would be better to wait and learn the result of the investigations of the new committee.

COUElCitioi HEATON said that in the absence of the chairman and vice-chairman of the committee he would take it upon himself to accommodate the Council, and withdraw the resolution regarding the augmentation of the brizade twRiR members.

Councillor Mosacs questioned the wisdom of instruct- ing the Borough Surveyor " to prepare a report on the situation and description of all hydrants (together with the size of the water mains) in the borough." He thought the waterworks engineer ought to prepare such reprt, as the Borough Surveyor a': present had more than he could do,and in addition the water works engin- eer should be mon qualified to make out such a report. Councillor PrmsteroN considered that the compiling of a report was ahsolutely necessary. Councillor MONKS proposed an amendment that the resolution instructing the Surveyor to prepare a report be withdrawn.

Councillor FIEATON observed that it was necessary that thP Borough Surveyor should visit every one of the hydrants for the purpooe of placing two rings of sets around those hydrants in unpaved streets. By so doing the hydrants would be easily found by any simply. minded person whenever it was necessary.

Councillor MoNgs thought it was not at all necessary that the Borough Surveyor should visit these places. It would be quite sufficient if he simply marked the spots upon the map. Councillor WOODS seconded the amendment, and Councillor ROBERTS supported. The last-named gentle- man remarked that for some time there had been consi- derable friction between the Fire Engine Committee and the Water Committee. Alderman FRANCOMB: It is not true; there is no friction. Councillor ROBERTS: It is no use your denying it; I know it is absolutely true. Proceeding, , Councillor Roberts said that once for all this sort of thing —this bad blood between the two committees—ought to be put a stop to. There wal3, without a doubt, friction between the committees, and the consequence of it was to be seen in the position in which the town stood that day. When any recommendation was made by the Fire Engine Committee to the Water Committee, the latter put their backs up at once; and it was a fact that the Water Committee did not yet know where all the hydrants were. Councillor BENNETT suggested that to expedite the business all the resolutions of the Fire Engine Commit- tee should be referred back.

I Councillor HEATON expressed his willingness on behalt I of the committee to withdraw also the resolution bay- ing reference to the Borough Surveyor. Referring to the capability of the committee and the brigade, he said that he had seen fires in Liverpool and other large towns but he had never seen a shop better saved than Skelton's. It was the object of all brigades, be thought, to protect the property adjoining a burning building, and the War- rington brigade had well succeeded in doing this. Coun- cillor Roberts was quite right in stating that there bad always been a certain amount of friction between the two committees. Communications had been addressed by the Fire Engine Committee to the Water Committee, but not the slightest notice had been taken of them, and they did not know to-day what hydrants had been put down. Nevertheless, he had pleasure in withdrawing the resolution alluded to by Councillor Monks. The Council, by their action, had apparently made the chair- man and vice-chairman of the Committee ill—(laughter) —for they had fal'en back upon him (Councillor Beaton) to conduct the minutes through the Council, thinking, no doubt, that he had better health to champion the cause. (Renewed laughter.) Nothing Councillor Woods could say would make him ill. He concluded by express- ing the opinion that if the councillors had not been so officious the fire would have been better attended to. Alderman Fnexcomia denied again that there existed any friction between the committees* The Water Com- mittee were very anxious to help the Fire Pugin() Onn,- mittee in every possible way, and had DO wish to prove obstructive. The Fire Engine Committee had only to send hydrants, and the Water Committee would put them in. They ought to carry on the town's business without friction, and so far as the Water Committee were concerned this was being aim, d at. The minutes with the withdrawn items eliminated were ,I passed unanimously.
OTHER COMMITTEES. The minutes of the Water Committee and the General Purposes Committee were passed without discussion.
THE COMMITTEE OF INQUIRY .INTO EFFICIENCY OF TUB FIRE

BRIGADE. At the conclusion of the public business the Council resolved itself into committee for the purpose of ap- pointing a committee whose duty it would be to consider the present state of the Fire Brigade,&c., as proposed by Councillor Skelton at the previous meeting of the Coun- cil. The gentlemen selected to form a committee were —the Mayor, ;the Deputy-Mayor, Aldermen Francomb and Hutchinson, and Councillors Hepherd, Lee, Evans and Woods.
