The birds were despatched on Friday, 21st inst. to the marking rooms of the Manchester Flying Club who took the charge of conveying them and of liberating them. div.head: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB SPORTS.
div.p: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB SPORTS.

At the time for the commencement of the programme provided for the Warrington Football Club Athletic Festival held on the Wilderspool enclosure last Friday,the weather prospects were not of the brightest, two smart showers having previously fallen somewhat to the detriment of the track which, nevertheless, was in good condition. There was a fair attendance which would have been greater but for the fact that so many people had left the town with the school trips and in other ways. The officials at the sports were :—Clerk of the 'course : Mr. T. Bowers ; starter : Mr. E. Kane judges : Messrs. J. Evans, W. Lomas, R. Andrews and E. Gilbert ; judge of boxing competition : Sergeant Major Haigh ; committee : Messrs. T. Davies,W.Hewitty IV. Hill, W. Hayes, F. Barber, C. Burton, W. Howard, J. T. Bate, and J. Lawless ; handicapper : Mr. W. Platt; hon. treasurer : Mr. T. Pemberton ; hon. secre- tary : Mr. J. E. Warren; assistant hon. secretary : Mr. S. W. Jeffery. The Widnes St. Mary's prize band was in attendance and provided spirited music during the intervals, under the conductorship of Mr. .I. J. Brady. The first item on the programme and moreover one which aroused an enormous amount oi interest was the 100 yards local foot handicap. In this race there were five heats representing 21 competitors, all of whom ran finely. The winners were as follows :—Beat 1, W. Hos- tron, Warrington St. Peters ; heat 2, A. J. Mrttrarn, Warrington F.A. ; heat 3, J. Cunningham. IVarrington F.O ; 4, T. Horan,Warrington, St. Peters ; 5, F. Broady, Wallington F.C. In the final, which was very hotly contested, the winners were J. Cunningham, Warring- ton P.C., Ist; T. Horan, Warrington St. Peters, 2nd; ,F. Broady, Warrington F.C., third. For this handicap , the prizes were—first, marble eight day clock with pair of military bronze figures; second, silver-plated dinner cruet ; third, silver-plated butter dish. Following this was the exhibition of cycle trick riding by %V. G. Hurst, the world's champion in this line. His display was truly marvellons,and contained feats which, might reasonably have been deemed impossible previ- ously. The machine which Hurst rode was a handsome well-finished, geared "ordinary," and evidently made of the best material judging by what it stood. ! In the 440 yards obstacle race which was the next item on the programme,the,e were two heats comprising ten competitors. The race was productive of mush amusement. and in heat 1, J. Turner, Northvvich was first ;T. Pownev, Warrington, second ; and J. Green Warrington, third. In heat 2, D. Gibson, Warrington, G. Long, Warrington, and H. Boyle, Warrington, were respectively first, second", and third. The final between these six was won by G. Long, Warrington, first ; J. Green, Warrington,second ; and H, Boyle, Warrington, third. For this race the , prizes were-Ist, reculator .clock : 2nd, four cup egg frame; 3rd,Doulton.warelvenuit barrel).

. . The cycle races in the sports were productive of a great amount of speculation, as some of the most famous riders in the surrounding district had been attracted by the circulation of the pr ze list. Race number one was the one mile handicap, con=isting of four heats and 30. competitors and the first and second in each heat com- peted in the final. Heat one saw R. J. Gledhill, OFthara R.C.C.,lstond B. N.wcomhe Warrington C.C.; 2nd heat two, T. Astill, Warrington C.O , first; W. Afghani, War- rington C.O , second ; heat three, J. Dootson, Horwich- C.C.,firs ; W. Sherratt,WidnesC.C., second ; heat four. G. H. Smith, Warrington C.C., first in a " canter," anti A. T. Daintith, Warrincton C.C., second. The final was splendidly contested, showing the riding powers of the respective champions to advantage. Astill, Warrington. from scratch, was first ; G. H. Smith, Warrington, second ; J Dootson, Horvtich, third. The prizes were —lst, English silver lever centre seconds chronograph ; 2nd, silver plated fruit stand ; 3rd, silver plated four bottle cruet.

Event 4 WAR a nine stone boxing competition (under A.B.A. rules) for a first prize of gold albert and slal ; cond, English peent lever. In the first round F. Snell, S wall Heath A.C., won against E. Hobson; S. Baker, Garston, won against H. Jackson, Manchester. In the second round Snell after a determined struggle won against M. Jeffers of Warrington. The final was just ass tough and was decided in favohr of Snell against Jack- son. Mancbester.

- There was only one heat and a dozen competitors in the 880 yards flat handicap for a Ist prize of engraved tea and reffi•r service : 2nd, six cup ege frame and spoons; 3rd,hutter dish. The winners were H. E. Daviefft West Cheshire Harriers, first ; E. Gordon. Liverpool H. and A F.C., second ; 3rd W. Price, Orfsird Harriers. A two mile bicycle handicap of three heats and over 30 compstitors was ridden for a marble and bronze clock as first prize ; spirit kettle on stand, second ; and silver- plated teapot, third. In heat 1, R. J. Gledhill, Oldham, was first ; J. Davies, Warringtnn. second ; F. Jackson, • Manchester 8.C., third. Heat 2 was won by B. New- combe, Warrington ; T. Astill, Warrington, was second; and J. Dootaon, Horwich C.C., third. In heat 3, F. Tomlinson, Halehank C.C., came out first ; W. Burton, North Liverpool 8.C.. second; and W. div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
THE LOCAL VETO BILL,
In the House of Commons on Wednesday, Sir John T. Brunner, M.P., presented a petition from the united temperance societies in Runcorn, in support of the Local Veto Bill. .

..,—.... TISE DISTRWT NURSE'S VI ORK. The report of the R,lncorn district nurse for June shows that up to the 24th ult, she had paid 279 visits to patients. The occasional visits numbered 105. DRUNKENNESS, _ . .

At Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday morning, Frederick James Parker, a seaman, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in High-st. at eleven o'clock the previous evening.—P.C. Gregory proved the case, and a fine of ss. and costs was imposed. VOLUNTARY SCHOOLS' COLLECTION. On behalf of the National acacia's, Runcorn, the annual sermons were preached on Sunday. The Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., vicar of Frodsham preached at the morning service, and in the afternoon a flower service was con- ducted by the Rev. W. H. Stables, M.A. The Rev. W. Hodgson, of Widnes, preached in the evening. The collec- tions amounted to about £l4. THE RUNCORN BRANCH OF THE S.P.G. In the "Runcorn Parish Magazine" for the present month, the financial report for the half-year ending June 30th, in connection with the Runcorn and district branch of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel, shows that the receipts amounted to £25 17s. 9d., which is a decrease on the amount raised in the corresponding period last year. THE FERRY. —THE CANAL TOLL DISCONTINUED. The toll for crossing the canal by the ferry between Runcorn and Widnes was continued until last Saturday, when the officials at Runcorn received instructions to discontinue the charge of one penny for crossing the waterway. This will reduce the return fare by 2d., and no doubt greater use will bo made of the ferry by the public. ' Tim WESLEYAN DAY SCHOOLS AT RUNCORN. On Monday, the Runcorn School Board took over the ,duties connected with what have been known formerly, SS the Brunswick-st. and Granville-st. Wesleyan schools. These will now be carried on by the School Board. The teaching staff remains as before. SPECIAL SERVICE AT THE MARINER'S CHURCH. At the Mariner's Church, Irwell-lane, on Sunday, a special service for bereaved mothers was held, and was well attended. An address appropriate to the occasion was given by Mr. David Smith. The choir, under the conductorship of Mr. George Sutton,efficiently rendered the piece,' Watching and Waiting." A SUCCESSFUL RUNCORN CHOIR. At the third annual tonic sol-fa festival of Manchester and district held at the Royal Botanical Gardens, Man- chester, on Saturday, the Runcorn Tonic Sol-fa Choir' under the conductorship of Mr. J. Holford, succeeded in carrying off the second prize in the adult choral compe- tition. There were eight competitors, and the distinc- tion gained is a most creditable one. Each choir sang a piece of its own selection, also the glee "Break, break (G. A. Macfarren), and a sight piece. The prize gained by the Runcorn choir was of the value of £5.

A RUNCORNIAN FINED FOR BETTING. a Nantwich Petty Sessions on Monday before Baron von Schroder and other magistrates, a number of per- sons were summoned for having used the ground of the Crewe Athletic Club for the purposes nf betting on the occasion of the annual sports of the Crewe Alexandra Athletic Club, on the 15th June. Am ,ngst those sum- moned was Mr. Albert Abel, of Rurn•orn. P.C. Hoole said he backed a bicycle rider named Dentith with the defendant at two to one.—The defendant pleaded guilty, and said he had accompanied his cousin, who was a bicycle rider, to the sports. He bad never previously made a bet, and it was a business entirely new to him. He was only setting down a few figures for another man and was a commercial traveller.—A fine of £1 and costs was imposed. ACCIDENT TO A PERFORMER AT THE THEATRE. A company of variety artistes have this week been performing at the Theatre Royal, Runcorn, and included in the company was a performer professionally called " Tarrosan, the Japanese Marvel." He was going through a number of feats on the slack wire on Monday evening, when suddenly he fell to the stage, a depth of seven or eight feet. His fall was a most awkward one, and it was soon apparent that he had sustained serious injuries. The curtain was dropped for a short time, but the entertainment which was nearing its close, was afterwards proceeded with. Dr. McLennan was sum- moned to attend the injured man and that gentleman was early in attendance. He found on examination that the man had received serious injuries to his back, the spinal cord having been injured. He was removed to his I idgings in Wellington-st., where he was attended to by Drs. McLennan and Mangan, hut on Wednesday it was found necessary to remove him to a Liverpeol Hospital. THE ATTEMPT TO COMMIT SUICIDE AT RUNCORN.

-- Samuel Glover, of Salkeld-square, Runcorn, whose wife is now undergoing a term of imprisonment, was brought up on remand at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Minday, charged with havinv• on the 24th June at- tempted to commit suicide.—P.C. BoJth repeated the evidence given in last week's " Examiner" as to finding the prisoner with his throat cut, and a table knife in his hand. On being charged with attempting to commit suicide,he said he was very sorry for what he had done. —Superintendent Atherton stated that the warder brought word from the doctor at Knutsford Gaol that the prisoner was quite sane during the whole time he had been in the prison.—Prisener said it was a sup of drink that caused it ; it was no use telling a lie about it. —The Chairman (Sir R. Brooke) said the magistrates had decided to give him another chance,and they hoped it would be a warning to him to keep off the drink. The Prisoner : Thank you, Sir. I hope it will be." Holt and Thomas Clarke, stewards, in which it was pointed out that £122 16s. had ben paid to sick members during the half-year, against £9O in the corresponding half of last year. There were now 286 adult members in the division.— A letter was read from Mr. Marshall, secretary to the Technical In- struction Committee, asking the Order to take part in the demonstration at the opening of the Institute on July 17th.—It was resolved to recommend the members to take part in the opening ceremony, earnest hopes be- ing expressed that the members would largely take part and thus show their appreciation of the services rendered by Sir John T. Brunner, who had so generously contri- buted to the building fund.—The election of officers for the next half-year was then proceeded with, the follow- ing being chosen :—Mr. Thomas Fleesom, W.P. ; Mr. Ernest Hobson, W.A.; G. div.head: PICNICS FROM RUNCORN.
div.p: PICNICS FROM RUNCORN.

There have been several picnics from Runcorn during the past week. On Monday the Sunday school teachers, choir, and workers in connention with the Runcorn branch of the Mersey Mission to Seamen had their annual outing to Chester. The journey was undertaken in wagonnettes, and the party arrived there about 12.30. After a lunch they proceeded up the Dee to Eccleston Ferry, a visit being paid to the Duke of Westminster's gardens. At 4.30 they departed for Chester again,where tea was partaken of. After a stroll round the ancient city the return journey was commenced. Runcorn being safely reached about 10.30. The picnic was a most enjoyable one notwithstanding the few showers of rain which were experienced. The arrangements, which were in the hands of Mr. Shaw (missionary), Mr. David Price, and Mr. Bvfleld, were most satisfactory.—The members of the Bible Class connected with Mill Brow Ragged School, and conducted by Mr. Smith and Mr. Cunning- ham, also had their picnic on Monday and proceeded to Chester. The party numbered about 30 and they spent the day in a most enjoyable manner.—A picnic in connection with the Camden Wesleyan Mother's meet- ing was held on Tuesday, when a party numbering 40, proceeded in a waggonette to Grappenhall. After a ramble round the village they proceeded in the wag- gonette to Latchford and Etockton Heath. Tea was provided at the latter place by Mr. John Lowe,formerly of Runcorn. The arrangements were made by Mr. and Mrs. Baxley and Mrs. Santley.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATU
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATU

SHIP CANAL TONTINE CLUB. On Tuesday evening the members of the Ship Canal Tontine Club met in the Club room, George and Dragon Hotel, Runcorn, when the quarterly dividend was dis- tributed. Subsequently the members spent some time in a convivial manner. A number of songs were given. and the son of the president of the club, Mr. J. Aryes, gave a.ventriloquist performance. THE MEASLES EPIDEMIC. . . .

This epidemic still prevails in the town, and although the deaths have not totalled those of the previous week, there are numerous cases, especially in the north end of the town. Several of the infants' schools continue closed, and on Thursday it was found necessary to close Shaw-street infant school in consequence ot the ' disease. SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A CHILD AT WESTON. On Wednesday evening, Edward Charles Wilding,aged five years,residing with his parents at Loot's Row-Weston Point, was playing in front of his home with spine other children when he was knocked down by a bicycle which was being ridden by a cyclist named Jones, of North- wich. The child was carried into the honse in an insensible state, and Dr. McKenzie, of Runcorn, was telegraphed for. Besides several internal injuries the boy's collar bone is completely severed from the breast on the left side. He lies in a very dangerous condition.

div.head: Busy TIMES AT RIINCORN DOCKS.
div.p: Busy TIMES AT RIINCORN DOCKS.

A pleasing feature in connection with the trade of the town, has been the increased trade at the decks. For some weeks past the number of vessels arriving at Run- corn has been exceptionally large, and on a visit being paid to the docks on Thursday, it was found that no fewer than 57 were in dock. This is considered to be the highest number for many years.

div.head: NORTHWICH ELECTION.
div.p: THE NORTHWICH ELECTION.

On Thursday morning a number of newspaper reports were current to the effect that Mr. James Verdin, of Northwich, had been asked to contest the Northwich division in the Conservative interest in the forthcoming election. This invitation was reported to have been made at a meeting of the Conservative Executive held at Northwich on Wednesday afternoon, at which repre- sentatives from all parts of the division were present. The representatives from Runcorn included Mr. E. Imison, J.P. (chairman of the Urban Council), Mr. F. J. Norman, J.P., Mr. J. W. Lightburn, Mr. Alfred Lightburn, and Mr. William Hankinson. On enquiry it was ascertained that no such decision had yet been come to, and that the report in question was prema- ture. Several likely candidates were present at the meeting, including Mr. Joseph Verdin and Mr. Hartley, of London,who delivered a short speech. But there was a disposition on the part of a number who were present including the Runcorn representatives, to avoid a con- test altogether at the present juncture. This feeling seemed to be so strong that It was decided to adjourn the meeting until Saturday after- noon, and accordingly no definite invitation was extended to anyone to stand. Whether there will be a contest in the division or not, will depend on the decision coma to at the adjourned meeting. Sir John Brunner will arrive in the constituency on Saturday, when he will address a meeting in the Gladstone Club, Northwich. The arrangements for a contest by the Liberal party are in an advanced state.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

A meeting of thia Beard was held at the Town Hall, Runcorn, on Tuesday evening. Mr. Thomas Handley, J.P., occupied the chair, and there were also present : Rev. Dr. Gastaldi' Mr. S. Taylor, J.P., C.C., and Mr. E. Imison, J.P.. and Mr. G. Moss (clerk). The School At- tendance Committee's minutes for June 18th, stated that thirty-five persons were summoned to attend before the committee, twenty-eight of whom attended. It was ordered that proceedings before the magistrates be taken in eleven cases. The attendance at the various public elementary schools had been considerably reduced owing to the prevalence of measles in the town. The minutes were passed on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by the Rev. Dr. Gaetaldi.—The Clerk reported that on the 15th June the accounts of the Board were audited by Mr. C. H. Joynson, Government auditor,who found them correct. It was also reported that it had been found necessary to close Mill Brow and Granville- street schools in consequence of the measles epidemic. Communications from the Education Department were read stating that it had been decided to waive the ex- amination of scholars at the Greenway-road Board (boys) se,hool, and Mill Brow Infant School. The grant would be on the same basis as that allowed last year.—The Chairman said it was very satisfactory that the two schools mentioned were exempt from examina- tim. It must be very pleasing to the Board that the Inspectors were satisfied by their casual visits to the schools.—lt was decided that the neat meeting of the Board be held on the 27th August, and that the scholars' holidays commence on July 17th. This concluded the business.

div.head: PENKETIL
div.p: PENKETIL

FIRE AT THE TANNERY.—On Tuesday morning an out- break of fire was discovered in one of the sheds at the works of the Penketh Tanning Co., Limited. The alarm was at once given and the fire was soon got under. The men worked: with great vigour, and but for the prompt measures taken a serious conflagration would doubtless have resulted.

LECTURE AT TUE Missroir —On• Monday evening last at St. Mary's Mission, the Vicar,the Rev. E. S. Jackson, M.A., delivered a lecture on " Mission Work in Central Africa." There was a small though appreciative au- dience.

SUNDAY SCHOOL Pircuic.—On Saturday, the annual picnic of the teachers and friends of the Wesleyan Sunday School took Place. It had been decided to pay a visit to the Children's Home at Edgeworth, near Bolton, and the morning turning out fine,a goodly number took advantage of the trip. The party left Penketh by the 9.43 train, and Bolton was reached about 11.30 a.m. Here wagonettes were in waiting to convey the holiday makers to the Home on the moors. The drive was a very pleasant one,and Victoria Park was visited en route. On arrival at Edgeworth the friends were received by Mr. A. W. Mager, the general governor of the Home, who spent the whole of the afternoon in showing the party through the Homes and explaining all the details ot the work there. After tea had been partaken of,the remain- ing time at the disposal of the friends was spent in wandering across the moors and in visiting the objects of interest around the Home. The return journey was commenced at 6.30 p.m., and Penketh reached at 10 3 O.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND THE GENERIL ELECTION.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND THE GENERIL ELECTION.
PREVIOUS PARLIAMENTARY ELECTIONS AT WARRINGTON.

Since 1868, when the first election after the passing of the Household Suffrage Bill was held, there have been Isix elections in Warrington, the Conservatives winning I four, and the Liberals two. From 1847 to 1888. Mr., afterwards Sir Gilbert Greenell, had represented War- rington, and at four elections he was returned unop- posed. Owing to the extension of the franchise, the Liberals thought that they had a better chance of cap- turing the seat, and Mr. Peter Rylands was nominated in opposition to Mr. Greenall. A very stiff fight ensued, and much to tne chagrin of the Tories, Mr. Rylands was returned by a majority of 18. At the succeeding election Sir Gilbert Greenall regained the seat, the fi<oirea being Greenall 2,3Bl,Rylands 2,201.T0ry majority,lBo. Not dis- couraged hy this result, the Liberals again contested the seat in 1880, Mr. J. G. McMinnies being the candidate nominated. The contest was a memerable one, and re- sulted in a crushing defeat of the Tory pary, The figures read : McMinnies 3,002, Greenall 2,473,Liberal majority, 529. In the last three elections the Conservatives have won. At the election on the 24th November, 1885, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., received 4,010 votes and Mr. William Crosfield 3,134,the former thus securing a major- ity of 776. At the next election,nn the 2nd of July,lBB6, Sir Gilbert received 3,717 votes, while his opponent,Mr. John Crosfield, had 3,216, the latter thus being in a minority of 501. At the last election, on the sth July, 1892, the present member, Mr. Robert Pierpojnt was returned by a majority of 585 votes. The figures were— Mr. Pierpoint, 3,843, Dr. Houston 3,258.

div.head: MUSIC IN THE PARK.
div.p: MUSIC IN THE PARK.

On Thursday next, Mr. T. J. Down's military band (conducted by Mr. T. J. Down) will play the following selection of music in the park (weather permitting), commencing at 7 o'clock :—March. 'Washington Post," Sousa; overture, " Tantalus- qualen," Suppe ; quadrille, " Chilperic," Godfrey; selection, "Sir H. Bishop's Songs," .fartmann ; overture, "Si retais Roi " (with Glockenspiel), Adam ; selection. " Cambria," Bonnisseau ; galop. " Lustice Briider," Faust ; hymn. " Lux Benigna,' Rev. J. B. Dykes (arranged by Mr. T. J. Down) : God Save the Queen. INTERESTING MEETING AT LATCHFO RD.

On Wednesday evening a meeting was held in the Temperance Hall, Latchford. of juvenile tern- plan, and the meeting was opened with Ringing and Drayer. The chair was taken by Miss E.l-Tough, chief templar The programme was a flower service. each member contributing a bouquet of flowers. all of which were tastefully arranged on a large table in the centre of the room. The Superintendent,Mr. L. r.llison, gave a short addreqy on flowerq, their influence on the heart and affections and on the formation of character. The following members gave readings Hough,Mr. J. Clarke,and A. Jones A recitation was given by E. Cliff, and , various songs were also rendered at intervals. Two members were appointed to convey the flowers to the hospital.
Our noted KID GLorms In all shades at Is. 614.,1r. and Es. 6d. per pair.—By Am', 17, Sankey-street, Wart ngton.

div.head: DAY, JULY 6 1895
div.p: DAY, JULY 6 1895
RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL,

A meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall, Runcorn, on Thursday morning. Mr. E. Imison, J.P., occupied the chair, and there were also present—Rev. Dr Gadstaldi, Dr. McKenzie, Messrs. P. Speakman, J.P. C.C., F. Wiswall, R. H. Posnett, J. Pritchard, J.Wilson, J. Jones, H. J. Grice, J. D. Bishrown, T. Dean, M. Sweetman, G. H. Kirkham, Mr. F. A. Lake (law clerk), Mr. E. Marshall (secretary), and Mr. M. Barker (sur- veyor).
THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN._

The report of the Medical Officer stated that the num- ber of deaths registered during the past month amounted to 47. Of these 19 were due to measles. 3 to scarlatina, 2to diphtheria, 4 to bronchitis, 2to pneumonia, and other diseases including one to heat apoplexy. The 47 deaths mentioned represented an average death rate for the twelve months of 29.6 per thousand. The number of births registered during the past month amounted to 36. The great increase in the death rate during the past month, it would be noticed, was almost entirely due to the presence of an epidemic of measles. This disease alone had increased the death rate by 12 per thousand per annum for thepast months. The epidemic produced as serious a falling off in the attendance at various infants' schools that with a view of diminishing the severity of the epidemic, be recommended the closing of a certain num- ber of these schools. The report was adopted, and it was also resolved on the motion of the Chairman that the action in closing the schools be confirmed.

div.head: HIGHWAYS- AND BUILDING commirrsE..
div.p: HIGHWAYS- AND BUILDING commirrsE..

It was recommended by this Committee that the ten- der of Messrs. H. Heyea and Co. to supply 40 tons of 4 " cube setts be accepted ; that the amended plan of Messrs. Hallding and Warburton of two houses proposed to be built in Norman-road be approved. Passed ontbe motion of Mr. Dean.

div.head: HEALTH COMid ITTEIC.
div.p: HEALTH COMid ITTEIC.

The Sanitary Inspector having reported the existence of nuisances at Camden Buildings, High-street ; at 3, Regents-street : 75, and 77, Church-street ;1, Egerton- street ; 44 and 44 Devonshire-Square ; 67, 69, 71, 73, 75, 77, 79, 81, Shaw-street, and the beerhouse known as the " Manchester House," Bridge-street, the Health Com- mittee recommended that notices be served for the abatement of the nuisances upon the owners, and that in the event of non-compliance with the committee's notices, legal proceedings be taken. They also recom- mended that the plan of the executors of the late J. Forster for the erection of a water closet at Millstone- yard, Mill-street be approved.—Mr. Wiswail moved and Mr. Once seconded the adoption of these minutes which were adopted.

WATER COMMITTEE.—TTIE WESTON SUPPLY% This Committee recommended that application be made to the Local Government Board for their sanction to the borrowing of a sum of £660 to be repaid in thirty years, for extension of existing water mains and laying of new mains in Norman-road, Moughland-lane, Heath. road, Greek-street, Hope-street, Queen's-road, Havergal- street, and Balfour-street ,• the purchase of six waste detecting water meters and an indicator to register the height of water in the Reservoir on Runcorn Hill and the enclosure of such Reservoir ; that the tender of Messrs. Simpson,Davies and Sons to supply 1.200 tons of Bridge- water Trustees' Worsley tip slack to be delivered in such quantities as may be required within 12 months at the Top Locks, Runcorn, or at the Runcorn Railway Station in the event of the Bridgewater Canal being frozen, be accepted ; and that the sum of £94 7s. 2d. for empties, ikc., in respect of the water rate for the quarter ending 24th June, 1895, be allowed.—Mr. Wilson moved the adoption of these recommendations, and in doing so, said that with the extension of property in Runcorn the committee had been obliged to take the action recommended in the first named minute. Mr. Wilson was proceeding to speak about the supply to Weston, when the Chair- man said as it was not on the Minutes it must be dis- cussed under general busines4.—This was afterwards done and Mr. Wilson said he just wished to point out this fact,that on referencia being made it was found that at the time when it was stated that 42 houses in Weston were without a supply of water, the supply to the main had been turned off for the purpose of repairs. He thought it was a little unfair to say that the Committee had no water to supply to Weston when the contrary was the case.—Mr. Posnett was of the opinion that the people should have lren notified when the water supply was to be turned off.—Mr. Grine thought that after the explanation the matter might be wisely left to the con- sideration of the Water Committee.—The Chairman said it would not be necessary to give any instruction to the Committee, and thespatter then dropped. MR. POSNETT'S MOTION. .

The Parliamentary and General Purposes Committee reported that having considered the matters referred to in Mr. Posnett's motion, they recommend as follows That application be made to the Local Government Bond under section 33 of the Local Government Act, 1894, for an order conferring pn the Council all the fol- lowing matters :—The appoilloment of overseers and assistant overseers and the revocation of appointment of assistant overseers; the powers, duties or liahilities of a Parish Council particularly those under section (6) 1 (a) (o) section 8 (1) h, i, and k, section 9 and section 14 of the Local Government Act, 1894. The committee consider the power to appoint assistant overseers of great importancn, as in this parish the election of assis- tant overseer is in the vestry with power for anyone to demand a poll. Such a method is the most unsuitable that could be devised for the election of an official. The powers of the vestry are needed as the Council having takna over the Burial Board under section 62 should have power to appoint salaries of cemetery officials without appealing to the vestry as required by the Burial Act, 1852, section 15. The power to accept gifts under section 8 (1) h, appears desirable in view of Sir J. T. Brunner's proposal to transferthe Guild Hall to the Council upon trusts.—These recommendations were agreed to without discussion. "THE BRUNNER GUILD HALL."

The Parliamentary and General Purposes Committee also recommended that the proposal of Sir J.T.Erunner, Bart., Ml'. to convey the buildings and land heretofore known as "St. John's Chapel and house" to the Coun- cil upon trusts, be accepted ; and that the premises be known as "The Brunner Guild Hall." The terms of the proncsed trust deed were submitted, and have already appeared in the " Examiner!' The committee further recommended that Sir J. T. Brunner, Bart.. M.?., Mr. Edwin Imison, and Mr. George H. Kirkham be appointed members of the committee of management on behalf of the Council.—Mr. Speakmatr proposed the adoption of the minutes, Dr. Gastaldi seconded, I and they were unanimously agreed to. The fol- lowing communication was read :—Writing on be- half of Sir John T. Brunner, Mr. R. W. Kettle stated that he was asked to say that as regards the points regarding the new hall, he consented to the requests of the General Purposes Committee. Sir Jnhn also wished him to say bow very much gratified he was by the kindly feeling shown in the wish that the hall should bear his name, and though he had been hesita- ting on the point, he had in the end felt that he ought to accept that kind pledge of friendship. He also ac- cepted with pleasure the nomination to act as one of the committee of management —Mr. Speakman thought they should tender to Sir John Brunner their hearty thanks for the building. He moved the following resolu- tion, " That this Council cordially thanks Sir J. T. Brunner for his generous gift, and sincerely hopes that he may be spared for many years to see it grow in use- fulness and in the apnreciation of those who meet within its walls."—Dr. Gastaldi .seconded the motion and it was carried unanimously.
THE TECHNICAL INSTITI7TE.

The Technical Instruction Committee recommended that a key and an illuminated address be presented to Sir J. T. Brunner on the occasion of the opening of the Institute ; and that application be made to the City and Guild; of London Institute to accept the Technical In- struction Committee of the Runcorn Urban District Council, as a committee for carrying on the Institute's examinations.—These minutes were moved by Mr. Wis. wall, seconded by Mr. Wilson. In supporting them, Mr. Bisbmwn said he ventured to say that whatever their political bias might be, they would all believe that Sir John Brunner had been a benefactor. They all fully appreciated what he had done in Runcorn, especially with regard to the Technical Institute. Soon after the inception of the scheme for a Technical Institute, Sir John tock the matter under his wing and in a nractical manner showed his sympathy with technical instruction The minutes were then passed.

TSB LTBRARY. The Library Committee recommended that SO volumes of new books as per list to be submitted be purchased ; and that the fee charged to persons living outside the district for the use of the lending library be reduced from ss. to Is. per annum. In moving the adoption of these minutes, Mr. Grine said he thought the Council would he of the opinion that it would be an advantage to the residents outside Runcorn to be able to borrow honks from the Library on payment of one shilling.— Mr. fliabrown seconded the resolution and congratulated the committee on coming to the decision they had done. The minutes were passed.

div.head: TRE FERRY SETTLEMENT.
div.p: TRE FERRY SETTLEMENT.

The minutes of the Finance Committee stated that the expenses of the deputation to London to meet the solici- tors to the London and North Western Railway Company and the Manchester Ship Canal Company re the Ferry amounted to £8 10s. Bd.—Mr. Speakman said it was only right that that at that stage some report of the de- putation should be given to the Council. It would be remembered that it was decided to join in an appeal to the Assize Courts for the ferry to be re;tittited as it was before the Ship Canal broke through it. But before going to the Assizes it was thought that a little negotia- tion would bring the whale trotter to a successful issue. He was glad to tell that Council chat AS a result of a con- ference at London they had been able to establish a high level approach at Runcorn, en that passenger steamers might come, and take passen. gess on bcard. There would be steps provided for those who wished to use the ferry. With regard to the ques- -1 than of an arnanach at Whine, it WRS estimated that it would cost £5O. After a long discussion, the Committee of the Council agreed that it was wise tn accept a sug- gestion for the Riincrrn Council to pay £l2 10s. towards the coat. He could say that they were received very cordially in London, and not only so but the Railway

Company sent free passes for them to go there. There- fore the cost to the Authority was very small. He had forgotten to say that the vexed question of the Man- chester Ship Canal Company's charge of one penny for crossing their waterway had now been done away with. —Dr. Gastaldi considered the settlement very satisfac- tory, and hoped the public would make greater use of the ferry in the future.—The minutes of the Finance Committee were then passed.
THE OPENING OF THE INsTrrum
The seal of the Council ;as affixed to an address to Sir J. T. Brunner on his opening of the Technical In- stitute, on the motion of Mr. G. H. Kirkham, seconded by Mr. M. Sweetman.

div.head: INSPECTOR OF NUISANCES.
div.p: THE INSPECTOR OF NUISANCES.

I Mr. Wiswall moved that Mr. James Percival be ap- pointed Inspector of Nuisances for a further period of one year at the present salary af £125 per annum, and that the consent of the Local Government Board be obtained to such appointment ; the year to date from July 4th, 1895.—Mr. Posnett seconded, Dr. McKenzie supported, and it was carried.
CONGRATULATIONS TO SIR J. T. BRUNNER.

The Chairman said there was an opinion in the town and one widely held by that Council that they ought not to let the honeur which had been conferred upon Sir John Brunner to pass unnoticed by the Council. It was not that they were obliged to follow the example of other places, but they had strong reasons for doing so. One of the most prominent was the great help Sir John Brunner gave during the past winter. There was no doubt that the distress would have been largely in- creased had not it been for his generosity. There was another reason, he had been mainly instrumental in the erection of the building which was shortly to be opened. They had also reason to be grateful to him for his help to the Council with regard to several matters which required attention in London. He had always rendered ready, willing, and very effective help. He (Mr. Liaison) had pleasure in moving " That this Council congratulates Sir J. T. Brunner on the honour which has been conferred upon him by her Majesty and earnestly hopes that he and Lady Brunner may be long spared to enjoy their distinction. —Mr. Pritchard said he seconded the motion with the greatest of pleasure. He referred to the gift of the Trades Hall by Mr. Brunner, and his generosity in contributing to the Pechnical Institute. They recognised in those facts an effort on the part of Sir John Brunner to distri- bute his wealth for the greatest benefit of the cemmu- nity.—Mr. Wiswall and Mr. Speakman, in supporting the motion, alluded in felicitous terms to Mr. Brunner's labours and generosity for the good of the town.—The motion was carried unanimously.

div.head: MOT/ON BY DR. OASTALDI.
div.p: MOT/ON BY DR. OASTALDI.

The Rev. Dr.--Ga;t-a.1.-zil gave notice that at the next meeting of the Council he would move that a memorial from the Council be sent to the Directors of the London and North-Western Railway Company urging the desirability in the interest alike of the said company and the travelling public, and above all the working classes, of a reduction in the existing charges for transit per Runcorn Bridge and Ferry, to issue tickets available either for bridge or ferry, and further to reduce the rail- way fares between Runcorn, Ditton, and Widnes.
A DEPUTATION THANKED.

Dr. Gastaldi moved, and Mr. Grice seconded, a vote of thanks to the deputation for their successful negotia- tions respecting the ferry.—Mr. Speakman and the Chairman acknowledged the compliment, the latter re- marking that he did not think it would be a desirable thing to permit themselves to become a mutual admira- tion society by continually patting each other on the back. (Laughter.) This concluded the business.

div.head: THINGS HEARD-AND SEEN AT RUNCORN
div.p: THINGS HEARD-AND SEEN AT RUNCORN
BY OUR RUNCORN CORRESPONDENT.

The air has been filled with ruuaours of dissolution during the past few days, and naturally the "things heard" have been chiefly with regard to forthcoming struggle. " Will there be a contest in the division ? " has been a query to which no de- finite answer was obtainable. That 1,255 majority of Sir John Brunner's at the last election, and the increasing popularity of the member for the divi- sion, seem to be thought by some to be sufficient to ward off a contest, but those who are supposed to know something about the inner workings of the opposite party appear to be quite confident of of a "fight." But the meeting of the Conservativel Executive on Wednesday, does not strongly indi- cate any anxiety for a contest. After a lengthy discussion the meeting was adjourned as there was a desire on the part of many, especially the Run- corn representatives, to throw up the sponge, and therefore a difficulty arose in selecting a candidate. Another meeting is to be held on Saturday when sonr..thing of a definite character may be expected. Should a candidate be decided upon, whoever that gentleman may be—whether he comes from London or elsewhere—there will at least be something to admire about his pluck in enterinc the field. I-le may rest assured that he will not catch the Liberal Iparty napping for all their arrangements for a contest are in "tipple pie " order.

A public testimonial to the Runcorn hero named Hughes, who it will be remembered, was presented with a medal and diploma at Liverpool a short time ago for his bravery, is being raised in the town, but as yet, it has received very meagre support. It is admitted on all hands, that the act was a most heroic one, and it well deserves recog- nition. In preventing a number of trucks from dashing headlong among his fellows who were then employed in the construction of the Ship Canal, he sacrificed both his legs. It is over two years since it occurred, and the greater part of that time he has spent in hospitals. He is still unable to work and his hopes of being able to support himself and his family are blighted. It certainly is a case in which the public of Runcorn should not shrink from raising a substantial testimonial, and it is to be hoped that the movement which is on foot with this end in view, will be liberally supported.

Salkeld-square has been well represented at the Police Court lately, On Monday a number of the inhabitants of the square figured at the Police Court on various charges and some are now being accommodated in Knutsford prison. One woman was committed for two months hard labour for neglecting her two children. The evidence clearly proved that she was a drunken and neglectful mother, and one distressing feature of the case was the fact that the husband was called upon to give evidence against his wife. This will certainly not conduce to their future happiness for the wife showed her resentment of his conduct by slapping his face as she was being removed from the dock to the cells below. Many encomiums were passed upon Sir John T. Brunner, MX ,at the meeting of the Runcorn Urban Council on Thursday when a vote of congra- tulation upon the honour which the Queen has con- ferred upon him, was under consideration. It may seem rather late in the day to pass such a resolution, but it was the first meeting, and consequently the first opportunity, the Council have had of doing so, since the conferment of the baronetcy. Sir John Brunner has proved himself a true philanthropist to the town, and the remarks which were made yesterday by.men of different political beliefs, and the unanimity with which the resolution was passed, were evidence of the high esteem in which he is held in Runcorn.

The report of the Medical Officer of Health which was presented at the meeting of the Runcorn Urban Council yesterday. showed, as was anticipated, a rather remarkable increase in the death rate. This was due to the wave of measles which seems to be passing through the town, and which has been the cause of a number of infant schools being closed. The disease first made its appearance in the southerly part of the town, but now it is raging in the north, and on Thursday the Shaw-street infant school which has been kept open all along, was closed for a short time. It is rather unfortunate for some of the schools that the disease should be prevalent at the present time, as the annual exam- ination of the scholars takes place within the next fortnight.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.
EXCITING INCIDENT NEAR RUNCORN.

On Sunday, the Blanche Rock (Captain Beahem), a vessel belonging to the Manchester and Bombay Steam Navigation Co., was coming up the canal from Jersey and had got just a little above Runcorn, when a man tried to get OR board, but he slipped and fell into the water. Two men in a small boat got hold of him but let him go, and the wian, who appeared to be fast drifting away would soon have sunk, had not the mate of the vessel (John file) immediately jumped into the water ard swam ashore with him. The man when rescued was in a very exhausted condition,and great praise is due to the mate for his plucky conduct. SERIOUS DAMAGE TO A STEAMER.

Shortly after eight o'clock on Wednesday evening the steamer "Ilelair "of Cardiff was proceeding on her out- ward journey to Kern, North Russia, from Manchester, when on reaching the Weston Mersey lock, which hap- pened to he opened at the time, she was carried by Oc- current, and came in violent collision with the lock wall, owing to the current causing her to sheer to star-board. The vessel's stern was twisted and large holes on her bows were made, in addition to a number of plates being stoved in. Considerable damage was also done to the timber work of the lock. The damage is roughly esti- mated at between £BOO and £1,009. The vessel is now lying near the lock and ii waiting for instructions as to . epairs.
the
FATAL RESULT OF A QITARRLL AT RUNCORN.--THE INQUEST.

_ Henry Kelly, 53 years of age, of 33, Fryer-street, Run- corn, employed as a labourer at the docks, died on Fri- day evening from injuries sustained dur;ng a quarrel, the previous Wednesday. Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, conducted an inquiry at Runcorn Police Court, on Saturday afternoon, concerning the death of the deceased. Superintend ent Atherton watched the case on I behalf of the police. Mr. Digges represented the Man- chester Ship Canal Company. The first witness called was Peter Bradley, dock labourer, of Back Mersey-street, who gave evidence of identification. He did not hear deceased and Kilkenny having words, but on coming down the stage he saw Henry Kelly lying under it. Witness picked him up, put him against a barrow, when he said he was not hurt. He accordingly left him there. William Henry Gibbs,39, Brackley-st., weigher at the Duke's Docks, said Kelly was of rather irritable temper. About 5.30 on Wednesday evening he was weighing clay,which was coming up in tubs from in a vessel. Kelly and Kilkenny and two other men were on the stage, on which the barrows were wheeled. Kelly and Kilkenny were tipping the tubs into barrows. He heard them having words with reference to their work. Kelly said he was as good a man as Kilkenny, which the latter denied. Deceased then threw out a challenge, and a fight commenced. Witness was unable to say who struck the first blow. A sailor and witness tried to separate them, when they broke away, and blows were again struck. He heard two of them, but they did not seem to be hard ones. The men closed in and Kelly fell backwards off the stage and Kilkenny after him on to the flags below, a depth of from seven to eight feet. In falling Kilkenny pulled the empty barrow after him,but witness could not say that it fell upon the men. He could not say who was uppermost on the floor. Peter Bradley and Bartley McManus were walling the clay, and they ran along the gangway, and he thought the latter was able tc break Kilkenny's fall, who did not seem to be hurt. Kelly's condition seemed serious, he bleeding from the mouth and nose. Witness reported the matter to Mr. Digges, and then, being under the impression that Kelly had been taken home, did not return to the scene. Witness thought deceased caused the quarrehas he was irritable all afternoon, mid challenged Kilkenny to fight. He had known Kilkenny for three or four years, and had never seen him quarrelling. Deceased fell with his head doubled under him. In his opinion, the bleeding was caused by the fall, and Rot through being struck. At first he thought he had broken his neck.

Hartley McManus, dock labourer, Cooper-st., said he had known Kelly and Kilkenny about 20 years. He was engaged walling clay about 16 or 17 yards from where they fell. Hearing the fall he ran and picked Kelly up. He asked him te come home, but as it was raining he declined. He never left him. They got home about nine o'clock.

_ Thomas btarkey,4,Mersey-st ,said deceased was a very quarrelsome man when at his work, but Kilkenny was very quiet. and would not fall out with anyone. Patrick Kilkenny, stated that he was a dock labourer, and lived at 17, Fryer-st, He had known deceased and had worked With him about 28 years. They had always been en friendly terms. On Wednesday evening, about 5.30, they were discharging the vessel J. Milton. They had been a bit of an altercation about holding the tubs. Witness went away to discharge his barrow load, Kelly following him. Deceased had to return first, and on their way back Kelly threw down his empty barrow on the stage, ran round to him and struck him twice. Kelly then challenged him to fight, when witness said " If you strike me again I shall defend myself and not allow you to strike me a second time." Kelly then rushed at him, and they "grappled," and in the struggle they fell down on the flags. It was all done in half a minute. Witness went down headforemost, and Kelly fell after, upon his arm. The barrow came on both of them, but he could not say whether or not it hurt deceased. Dr. Mangan, deposed that he had made a post-mortem examination,and found that death was due to a fracture of the left side of the skull, and the base also. He had heard the evidence as to his falling from the stage on the flag pavement, on the side of his head, which would account for the injuries found. The injury could not be due to a blow. He might add that there was a contusion of the eye, so that the man was struck previous to the injury to the skull. He had a black eye on the opposite side to that on which he fell. The jury, after a few minutes' deliberation in private, stated that their verdict was that Kelly was accidentally killed by falling from a stage whilst struggling with Kil- kenny.

div.head: BRUNSWICK WETLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. THE 95TH ANNIVERSARY.
div.p: BRUNSWICK WETLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. THE 95TH ANNIVERSARY.

Brunswick Wesleyan Sunday school is the eldest and the largest Sunday school in Runcorn, and the anniver- sary is always regarded as one of the chief events of the year. On Sunday, the 95th anniversary was celebrated, and one of the foremost preachers in Methodism—the Rev. S. Chadwick of the Leeds Mission was engaged as the preacher for the occasion. The commodious St. Paul's Chapel was well filled, morning and evening, and the earnest and eloquent discourses of tbe rev, gentle- man were listened to with great attention. Special hymns and anthems were sung by the choir and scholars in a most creditable manner. The choir WRS under the conductorship of Mr. R. Morris, and the organ was pre- sided at by Mr. Grine. The collections during the day realiz^el £47.

On Monday evening another service was held in the chapel, when the chair was occupied by Councillor Col- lier. Amongst those on the platform were the Revs. S. Chadwick (Leeds), S. F. Collier (Manchester Mission), T. Brackenhury, G. H. Tite, R. Renton (Frodsham), Messrs. P. Speakman, J.P., C.C., S. Taylor, J.P., C.C., F. J. Norman, J.P., J. Simpson, R. H. Posnett, E. Tay- lor, T. Simister, G. Bellamy, J. R. Frith, J. Bazley, A. Norman, R. Rawlimn, and G. Millington. There was a large eongregatian. After devotional exercises, the Rev. T. Braekenbury said he was sure the announce- ment that Mr. Collier was to be chairman would be acceptable to everyone there, and that they would give him a welcome. Mr. Collier briefly addressed the meeting.

The Rev. S. Chadwick said the subject he was about to I deal with was not to be an address on" Sixes and Sevens" but a sermon. Be said there was a general belief that long sermons were not popular but he could say that when he wanted to get a larger congregation that' usual he was only to announce that he was going to preach for an hour. He had come to the conclusion that It was a fallacy about the unpopularity of long sermons. His text was taken from Revelation xiii. c., 18v., which was "The number of the beast is the number of a man, and his number is 666." At the outset he gave numerous instances in which the phrase "big number is 666" had been applied, by bitter enemies, to notable persons for Centuries past. He said the beast mentioned, whose number was 666 was not one bat three. The first beast was the old serpent, which was called the Devil and Satan; the second beast was the one that rose up out of the sea and sat upon the throne ; and the third came out of the land and was in appearance like a lamb. He believed John had in his mind when he summed up the three beasts as one, the trinity of evil, in contrast to the trinity of good in the Godhead. There Was to be pre- pared warfare between the two until the kingdom of darkness was overthrown. But what was the meaning of 666? They understood that to the Eastern mind and especially to the .Tows figures were parables, and to the Jews 6 was always the unlucky number. They assumed that the highest point of per- fection apart from God was six, and that it took a God to make a seven. The preacher proceeded in A most in- teresting manner to point outfthat the things of this earth belonged to the sixes—they were not complete. Be referred to the advance in science and also in philosophy which was supposed to carry them farther than science. The modern gospel, apart from Christianity could be re- sumed up in three words : economics, sanitation, and education. He believed in all three, but these, he con- tended, were not sufficient for the perfect happiness of mankind. In order to secure peace in this world and everlasting felicity it was necessary for them to become the disciples of Christ. Then they would become seven and not six. In conclusion he urged the importance of his bearers examining themselves in order to ascertain whether they were included amongst the sixes or the sevens. (Applause.) The Chairman, in asking for a liberal collection, said there were 605 scholars and teachers in connection with 13runawick Sunday school. The average attendance was 400, and the annual cost to maintain the school in a state of efficiency was £65. The Rev. S. F. Collier said he was sorry to state that Gipsy Smith was unable to be present owing to family trouble, but on some future occasion he would be with them. The speaker spoke of the interest he had takenl in Runcorn, in consequence of having been an old Sun- day school scholar at Brunswick,Camden, and Nelson-at. schools. He wished them every success in their Sunday school work. (Applause.) A vote of thanks was accorded the Rev. S. Chadwick, and the Chairman, on the motion of Mr. R. H. Posnett, seconded by Mr. T. Si mister, and supported by the Rev. T. Brackenbury.—The Chairman, in reply, announced that the collections had realised £67. It Was a happy coincidence, six and seven once more. (Laughter.) The pronouncing of the doxology concluded the meeting.

MILITARY SIGNALLING BY WARRINGTON YOU:INTERIM —Captain J. A. Edelsten, Ist Vol. Batt. Prince of Wales Volunteers, South Lancashire Regiment, in command ot the signallers of that battalion, Warrington.gave his men (10) a treat on Saturday. They proceeded in a brake to Halton. On arrival they were immediately set to work flags, some on the top of the old castle,others at different posts in the vicinity, sending and taking military mess- ages till 6 30. when they again assembled at the Norton Armsflotel, and sat down to a substantial knife and fork tea, kindly provided by Captain Edelsten. Sergeants Headland and McHugh were with the party,and assisted Captain Edelsten in carrying eut the work. Captain Edelsten after tea was called away on urgent private business, thus leaving Sergeant Headland to set the men ts work again till nine o'clock. Mr. Birch, the landlord of the Norton Arms, was formerly an icetructor of the same Company.

The spring and summer months are, from a sanitary point of view, among the most important of the year. OVERCROWDING OF 'Buses. At the Warrington idoreugh Court on Monday, before the Mayor and Mr. F. Monks, William Connor, 'bus driver, 85, Knutsford-road, was charged with allowing his 'bus to be overcrowded on June 22nd. P.C. Forster said that at a quarter-past eleven on the night in ques- tion he saw the defendant driving a 'bus in Sankey.e. The 'bus, he could see, was overcrowded ,and he stopped it to count the passengers. He found that there were 17 in the 'bus which was registered for only 12.—The defendant said that a number of young fellows got in land would not get out, although he requested thee, to do. The Bench inflicted a fine of ss. and costa.—Alf red Millett,lB4,linutsford-road, was charged with committing a similar offence on the same night. P.C. Forster, who also proved tbis case, said that there were twelve on the waggonette, which was orly registered for ten. The defendant was fined in a similar amount to the last case. STRANGE CONDUCT IN A PUBLIC-HOUSE.—Jesge Plant, 53, Green-st., ironworker, and Thomas Greenhalgh, labourer, of 10, Clegg-it., were charged at the Warring. ton Borough Court, on Monday, before the Mayor and Mr. F. Monks, with stealing and receiving from the White Hart Hotel, Sankey-street, on Saturday afternoon a quantity of bread and ham, valued at 45., and also a door key.—Both defendants pleaded guilty.—Detective- Inspector Spinks stated that Greenhalgh was brother-in- law to Plant. At about 20 minutes past four o'clock on Saturday afternoon the defendants entered the White Hart, and were supplied each with a drink. Plant was seen to go towards the larder, which was locked, and then return to the room he had left. An assistant of Mrs. Brierley saw Plant go the larder again, and }incline a loaf in his possession, took it from him and called Mrs. Brierley's attention to the defendant's behaviour. When Mrs. Brierley went to the safe in the larder she found that Alb. of ham had been abstracted, and that a loaf was missing. At that time witness happened to be passing the White Hart, and being called into the house by Mrs. Brierley he entered, and found the defendant Plant sitting at a table with a piece of paper before him. which had been stained with barn Mrs. Brierley told witness that it was not the first time Plant had done this kind of thing, and asked the latter to hand over the key at once. She said that if he gave her the key and quitted the house she would say nothing more about the matter, seeing that he (Plant) was apparenqy a respect- able man. Plant made a search of his pockets, but did not produce the key, and then witness searched him,hut not very closely, not wishing to be too severe. The key could not be found, however, and Plant left the room. Witness followed him, and after he had joined another man on Bank Quay Bridge, he (the Inspector) brought him back to the White Hart. Here he again searched him, b t much more closely, and succeeded in finding the key in the inside waistcoat pocket. When asked the names of his companions Plant refuse( to give them. When charged with the theft, he replied, " I took the bread, key, and the ham, and gave the ham to Greenhalgh, who went up Golhorne-et." Witness had been unable to find the ham, hut the stolen loaf he pro- duced.—Auswerine Mr. Monks, he said that it was not a practical joke of Plant's. The defendant had done a similar thing before, but Mrs. Brierley had not thought fit to prosecute him, on account of his apparent respect- ability. The defendants were not in want of money,for each of them possessed more than 3s. when searched.— Both defendants expressed their sorrow to the magis- trates for what had occurred, and attributed their action to the fact that they were intoxicated at the time.—Plant was fined £l, OT One month's hard labour, and Greenhalgh sa. and costs, or seven days.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH COURT. FRIDAY. —Before Mr. J. Burgess (chairman), and Mr. S.

Wright. STEALING FLOWERS FOR WALKING Day.—Walter and Thomas Sherratt, boys, 33, New-road, Latchford. were charred with stealing on the morning of Friday the 28th, a quantity of flowers from the gardens of Peter Shakes- shaft and Peter Lamb,Knutsford-road.—P.C. Bell stated that he was in Knutsfo.id-rnad at 5 o'clock on Friday morning. when he saw the lads come out of a garden. He watched them enter another and take some of the flowers. Witness then went to them and brought both to the Police Station. The people who owned the flowers were unwilling to prosecute.—Both defendants were very repentent in court, and said that they had taken the flowers because they wanted some for Walking Day. —The Magistrates dealt leniently with the offenders by dismissing them with a caution. SATTIRDAY.—Before Messrs. John Burgessi(in the chair) and Samuel Wright. ALLEGED THEFT.—John Macdonald was charged with having stolen on the 13th June from a common lodging- house at Clothall-yard a man's shirt, valued at is. 6d.— Prisoner was committed to the Liverpool Quarter Ses- sions for trial. KEEPING DP WALKINO DAY.—For being guilty of drunkenness and disorderly behaviour on the previous day, Martin Cosgrove and Ann Donlan were each fined 55., or in default of payment, seven days in gaol. A MILITARY DESERTER.—Patrick McDermott was charged with having deserted from the Ist Dublin Fuel- Hers, and was remanded to Strangeways Gaol to await a military escort. MoNDAy.—Before the Mayor (chairman), and Mr. F.

Monks. DRUNKENNESS .—For this offence, committed in Peter- st., en Saturday night, Robert Porter, of no address,was fined ss. ; for the same offence, committed in Bridge-st., on Saturday night, Peter Carroll, and Annie Grey or Skelly, were discharged with a caution, and fined 53. and costs respectively ; James Mullins, of Lower Walton, was fined 2e. 6d., for being drunk and disorderly in vriars Green, on Sunday morning; Thomas Williams, 18 Hardy-st., was fined 53. and costs, for committing this offence in John-st., on June 22nd; Catherine Connolly, Pilkington's-court, was discharged with a caution, for being drunk and disorderly in Fennell-et.. on June 24. ASSAULT ON A WOMAN.—Sohn Owen, 49 Foundry-Mt., ' charged with assaulting Sarah Whittall, in Win- w. •-st., an Saturday afternoon.—r.c. Raper stated ths, he saw the prisoner standing by the Ray Horse Inn. and appeared tobe having hot words with the corn- plait t. After a lengthy dispute, he gave the woman , a sea blow in the right eye, knocking her on the grounu, and causing her to be in an unconscious condi- tion for some time. Witness took him in cuatody, and when charged with the offence, he said that the woman had asked him for some money.—The prisoner did not ,env the assault, hut said that the complainant had struck him first.—The Bench inflicted a fine of 51. in- cluding casts, OBSCENE LANGUAGE.—Kate Lally, 21 Havdock-st., was fined 24. 61. for using obscene and profane language in Haydock-st., on June 23.—P.C. Turner proved the
case. STONE TEROWING.—Herbert Wilcox, 84 Knutsford- road, was ened is. for throwing stones in Knutiford.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 6, 1895.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 6, 1895.

the bead —Mr. Lake for the defence said be did not know that he could suggest any proper excuse for the assault, except that there had been some ill feeling. Be (Mr. Lake) could only ask the maaistrates to be lenient, as the assault had been done in a moment of irritation. —A fine of 53. and costs was imposed. NEGLECT OP CHILDREN.—TWO MONTHS' BLED L113013H. —Michael Corcoran and Ann Corcoran, his wife, of 2, Salkeld-square, Runcorn, were both charged with hav- ing illtreated and neglected their two children, named Mary Ellen, 5 years of age, and Michael 11 months.— Mr. Allen, solicitor, Runcorn, said he appeared to prose- cute on behalf of the National Society tor the Prevention of Cruelty to Children. The neglect of the two children in question was of a serious character. They were neither properly fed, nor properly clothed,and the house was in a most shocking and dirty condition. The per- sonal condition of the children was also very bad. The female defendant was a drunken woman and had ap- peartd before the Bench on fourteen occasions for drunkenness and other offences. The male defendant earned 243. a week and he did not seem responsible for the neglect of the children.—lnspector McAteer deposed that he visited the defendant's house on the 20th of the previous month in company With Constables Gregory and Richardson. tie found the eldest child lying on a few filthy rags upstairs. It was almost alive with ver- min. There was no furniture in the house, no food, and no fire. Before going into the house he saw the female 1 defendant but she went away. When she did return she was under the influence of drink. He remonstrated with her a long time about her habits and the state of the children. ''She stated that she could not help it, and that she had no time to look after them. He had made special inquiries about the male defendant and he was led to believe that he was a most respectable man. His wife drank and squandered away his money.—P.C. Richard- son and Sergeant Lee gave corroborative evidence.— The male defendant stated that he gave his wife on an average between Ih3. and 204. per week. She did not spend it properly. He had given her money to buy bread, and she had spent it drink—The female defend- ant was then charged with being drunk and disorderly in Salkeld-square on the 17th inst. and the case was proved by P.C. Wylie.—The Chairman said that the female defendant had kept her children in the most dis- graceful state and she would be sent to prison for two months' hard labour. The charge against the male prisoner was withdrawn.—The female defendant on being removed from the Court said, in a loud voice, she could stand the sentence, and would soon be able to get over it, and do two months more when she had come out. She then struck her husband and said she would do " two more "for him. _ _....

CARD PLAYING.—Seven Runcorn youths named William Ashbrook, 26, Okell-street ; Thomas Gregory, court off Church-street ; Henry Lydiate, 30, Bridgewater-street ; John Lewis, 14, Taylor's-row ; William Kelsoe, 5, Fox- street ; Thomas Baker, 22, Surrey-street ; and Robert Bennion, 10, Surrey-street ; were all charged, and pleaded guilty to, gaming with cards in Cawley-street on the 23rd inst.—lnspector Hicks stated that about four o'clock on Sunday, the 23rd June, in company with several constables, he proceeded to Cawley-street, and there found the seven defendants playing cards. As soon as they saw the police, they ran away. Three of them were caught, and the others were known. There were numbers of complaints being made about this Sun- day card playing. Tney frequented Runcorn-hill, and the old brick field, and their conduct was most disgrace- ful. The Chairman said the magistrates were deter- mined to put a stop to it, and each defendant would be fined 103. and costs or in default of payment fourteen days' imprisonment. THE MUZZLING ORDER. —Henry William Jewke3, Hal- ton-road, Runcorn was fined ss. including costs for al- lowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled. OBSCENE AND PROFANE LANGUAGE.—Henry Lyne, Salkeld-square, was fined 103. and costs for using ob- scene and profane language on the 23rd June.—P.C.'s I Richardson and Wylie proved the case.—Mary Ann Glover, Salkeld-square, made her 12th appearance be- fore the Bench, and was charged wild using obscene and profane language in Salkeld-square, on the 23rd June. She was fined 103. and costs or in default 14 days im- prisonment. She went to gaol, and stated that her chil- dren could now be sent to the Workhouse.—Harriet Bax- ter, Mersey-st. (31st appearance), was summoned for a like offence on the 21st June, and was fined 103. and costs or in default of payment 14 days' imprisonment. D RUNKENNESS.—For being drunk and disorderlyaoseph Reyes, labourer, Halton, was fined 53. and costs ; and Catherine Bowden, for being drunk and disorderly in Mersey-st., on Sunday, was fined 103. and costs; Cathe- rine McConn (16ch appearance),was similarly dealt with for a like offence in Salkeld-square. THEFT OF POTATOES. —Benjamin Goodall. labourer, Clifton, was charged with having on the 29th June at Clifton, stolen eight pounds of potatoes growing in a field belonging toJoseph Stokes. Prisoner pleaded guilty. —P.C. Morris, stationed at Weston stated that about 11 45 on Saturday night he was on duty at Clifton when he saw the prisoner in. a potato field belonging to Mr. Joseph Stokes. Be watched him for some time and Saw that he was pulling them up and putting them in a bucket. Witness called to him, and he reply it was all right, he was only getting a few potatoes. Be had about eight pounds in the bucket. Prisoner told him that he wanted them for his Sunday's dinner. He was hard up and it was poverty which caused him to steal them.— Mr. Joseph Stokes stated that for the past twelve months potatoe stealing had been going on from his farm repeatedly. He had missed as much as a sack of potatoes at a time. They had been taken from the fields and from the hoggs. He had heard that tee prisoner had been out of work for some time. The magistrates said they were disposed to deal leniently with the prisoner as it was his first offence. He would be fined 53. and costs or Henn days hard labour. CHARGES OF ASSAULT. —Martin Gilligan, Fryer-street, Runcorn, was siimoned for assaulting Charles Rice at Weston, on the 28th June. The magistrates considered there was a dlubt in the case, and dismissed it.—A sailor named Frank Courtney was originally charged with unlawfully and indecently assaulting Eleanor Russell, a girl nine years of age, the previous day, but this was reduced to a charge of assault only. Eieamor Russell stated that she lived with her parents at 23, Collier-st. On the previous night she was picking flowers in a field near Top Loci's in company with a girl named Mary Guest. The prisoner came to them, and gave each of them a penny, telling the girl Guest to go and buy some swsets. He took witness into a shed and there assaulted her. After evidence by May Guest,Mrs. Guest, Mrs. Russell,and Inspector Hick s,the magistrates , helight it was insufficient to convict the prisoner, and discharged him.

DRUNKENNESS.—F-o.rWini'dr-u-nic—in Fennell-st., on Monday, Thomas Flannery, was fined 53. and costs. For committing the same offence at 5.10 a.m., on Tuesday morning, in Bank-st., was fined ss. and Costs. THURSDAY. —Before Mr. S._Chandley (chairman) and the

Mayor. Aworiaim DESERTER..—AIbert Lumley was remanded to Strangeways goal to await an escort for being a deser- ter from Her Majesty's let Derbyshire Regiment stationed at Dublin since the Ist July.—Defendant pleaded guilty and the case was proved by Detective Sergeant Monaghan who was granted the usual re- ward. A ROUGH CUSTOMER.—Patrick Lyton, a rough looking individual, was charged with assaulting and beating Jeffrey Woodhouse on the 29th April.—Mr. Woodhouse, who is the landlord of the " Lower Angel," stated that on the 29th of April he was standing in the bar when the prisoner came up and asked for liquor. He was re- fused being under the influence of drink at the time. Prisoner also refused to go out and sat down.whereupon complainant gave him a light touch with a child's whip. This enraged prisoner who picked up a pint glass and threw it at complainant who was struck on the arm in warding the blow from his face. The glass splintered and cut witness's arm and head, causing him to go to the Infirmary to have the former stitched.-1 woman who was in the public-house :at the time gave corroborative evidence.—Detective Sergeant Monaghan said that on the day of the assault he was called in the" Lower Angel" and saw complainant with his arm bleeding and the broken glass about. Prisoner had disappeared but witness got a description of him which enabled him to apprehend the prisoner in Horsemarket-street on Wed- nesday. Fie was identified by Woodhouse.—Prisoner who averred that the glass was knocked out of his hand was fined 20s. and costs or in default 21 days' hard labour.
WARRINGTON cOUNTY PETTY SESSIONS._
WEDNESDAY.—Before.Mr.G,Comber (chairman) and the
Rev. G. F. Roberts.

DRUNK AND DISO-11.E.R-LY..--IHenry 'Tomlinson was fined ss. including costs for being drunk and disorderly in Poulton,on the 28th June.—Michael Rock was fined 40s. and costs,or one month hard labour for being drunk and disorderly in Newton on the 2nd July. ASLEEP IN CHARGE.—Robert MeQuinn was mulcted in a penalty of 54. and costs for being asleep in charge of a wagon in Sankey-road, an the 7th June. Dens AT Lamm—James Smith was fined ss. including costs for allowing a dog to be at large on the 21st June last ; Frederick Hughes for committing the same offence on the 19th June in Penketh, was fined a similar amount. ASSAULT.—Elizabeth Bingham was charged with hav- ing on the 27th June in Sankey, assaulted and beaten Harriet Bayley. Defendant pleaded guilty. Mrs.Bayley said that on the day in question defendant struck her in the stomach and knocked her down. She then caught her by the hair and struck her in the eye making it black.—Defendant was bound over to keep the peace for three months. TEMPORARY AIIITIORITY.—WaIter Kerfoot was granted temporary authority to sell at the" Dog and Partridge," Paddington. BREAKING AND ENTERING.—MiChEeI Joyce was charged with breaking and entering the dwelling house of Hobert Walker, 17 Heath-street, Golberne, on the 29th June, with the intent of committing a felony.—Robert Walker the complainant, a middle-aged man described as an ex- cavator stated that on the night of the 28th June or the next morning he was awakened by hearing a noise in the room. He looked and saw the prisoner creeping about the room. Witness got up and found the prisoner under the had and pulled him out. He was detained by witness until the police came when Sorgeant Young re- ceived the prisoner in custody. Prisoner had neither boots nor clogs on and it was afterwards discovered that the scullery window was opened downstairs.—Emily Walker, 18, daughter of complainant, stated that the night of the 28th she made the windows and doors fast and with them the scullery window. In the morning she was awakened by hearing her father say there was some one in the room and going to her father's apartment she saw the latter standing over prisoner who was on the floor. She then went for the police and brought Ser- geant Young.—Prisoner waslcommitted;for trial,after the hearing of Sergeant Young's evidence, to the Liverpool Assizes.

SATURDAY.—Before Messrs. T. J. Gillespie (in the chair), T. D. Grimke-Drayton, J. L. Wood, C. B. F. Borron, and S. Brown. DRUNKENNESS.—The following persons were fined 53. and coats for having been drunk and guilty of disorderly behaviour at divers times and places.—Martin Davies, Richard Battersby, and Thomas Hill.—Fines of 2s. 6d. and costs were also inflicted upon Patrick Dunne, John Flaherty, Thomas Mellin, and Patrick Donnelly.—Mary Gibbons, who was charged with a similar offence was dismissed. ALLEGED BURGLARY.—MichaeI Joyce was fined ss. and costs for a similar offence, and was also charged with having burglariously entered the dwelling-house of Robert Walker, 17, Heath-place, Golborne. at 1.10 a.m. or. the 29 h June, with intent to commit a felony. The case was remanded to the County Petty Sessien3, to be held at Warrington on Wednesday. Dons Al' LARGE —Vernon Smallwood was charged with having allowed his dog to run at large unrnuzzled at Newton, and was ordered to pay the costs, 3s. 6e. ASSAULTS—James Hill was charged with having as- saulted Samuel Forster on the 17th June at Gelborne.— Complainant stated that he went to a public-house in Golborne with another man. When he entered the house defendant rose from his seat and struck him (witness) violently in the face. He (witness) had not provoked him in any way. Witnesses were called to prove this, and a tine of 20s. and costs was inflicted upon defen- dant who did not appear.—Frank Charles, who was charged with a slimier offence upon William Gloucester, was heund over to keep the peace for three months in a sum of £5 and was ordered to pay the costs. INFRINGEMENTS OF THE WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT. —George Waywell was charged with having had in his possession on the 6th June, at Newton, several sacks ot era' which were under weight. Defendant was fined 51. 'nettle hie cests.—George Naylor was charged with hav- ing had in his possession at Newton, on the 6th June, certain measures which were unjust, for which he was fined 20s and costs.—William Parkinson, Buttonwood, and John Cooper, Buttonwood, were each fined 103. and costs, and George Gleave, Buttonwood, was fined 20s. and costs for similar offences.—lnspector Spencer prose- cuted in each case. DAMAGING A FENCE.—Richard Roberts, Arthur Critch- IPS. and Herbert Froegart were charged with having maliciously broken a fence, value is., the property of the Vulcan Foundry, Earlestown, on the 12th June, for which they were ordered to pay the damage and costs each. DESTRUCTIVE PROPENSITIES.—WiIIiam WillStaßley was charged with having done damage to certain roots, to the amount of 34.. the property of Richard Evans,on the 24th May, a,- Newton. Be was further charged with baying on the same day wilfully lamed a certain hen, the property of Edwin Bealby.—Defendant was fined 103. and ereits for the two offences. ALEEGED THEFT OF TIMBER —William Bennett was charged with haying stolen four wood rafters, the pro- perty of George Bayley'e executors, between the 17th and the 20th June, at Newton.—Witnesses were called, and defendant was ordered to come up for judgment when called upon, and to pay the costs. I SHOCKING CRUELTY TO eBILDREN.—WiIIiam Henry Andrews end Mary Ann, his wife, who live at 120, Mersey-street, Newtor,were charged with having cruelly ill-treated and neglected their children on.the 25th June. Mr. J. W. Knowles prosecuted.—lnspector McAteer said that he visited the house in company with P.C. Dixon at 2 p.m. on the day in question, and he found five children Edith 11, William Matthew 9, Charles Edward 6, Lily 4, and Rose 1 year and 11 months old, who were in the front kitchen on the floor. All the children looked desti- tute and presented a most miserable appearance. They were also naked, and were covered with vermin. He had not been in the room long when the mother came in drunk. On the following day he again visited the house in the company of the same officer and found no bedding of any description except a few rags, and the only articles in the house were a jug., a tin can containing beer, and 29 empty porter bottles. He weighed the youngest child Rose in the presence of the constable and the parents, when he found that she only weighed 13 pounds, whereas a child of her age should weigh 231 b. Sqz. Both the parents were brought before Mr. J. L. Wood on the previnue Wednesday and had been re- manded till that day (Saturday).—P.C. Dixon corrobor- ated the last witness's statement.—Several witnesses were called to prove the drunken habits of the two de- fendants, and their negligence to their children—The defendants, who expressed their sorrow, were each sent to gaol for three months with hard labour.
