A PREMATURE CLAIM BY A WARRINGTON GROCER.—MY. John Burgess, wholesale urocer, Bridge Foot, Warring- I ton. claimed the sum of 12s. the value of two empty casks from Mrs. Eliza Harrison, shopkeeper, Ship-st., Frodsham.—Mr. Burton, solicitor, Runcorn, appeared for the defendant.—Mr. John Ashton Burgess said he was a traveller for his father, wh,a was the plaintiff. On April 16'ch, 1889, he received an order from the defend- ant fora barrel of syrup and also one of treacle. The goods were delivered, but the barrels, which were taken off the invoice on the settlement of the account some years ago, had not yet been returned. Six years was a most unreasonable time to keep the casks. They had applied to the defendant repeatedly for them hut had been unable to get satisfaction.—Mr. Burton for the defence stated that the order was given for 56Ibs. of syrup and 561bs. of treacle, but instead of receiving that amount, two casks each containing over two cwts. were delivered. The defendant was only a very small shop- keeper, and had been unable to sell it.—Mrs. Harrison confirmed her solicitor's statement, stating that she did not sell a penny worol of treacle im a month. The casks were only about half empty.—His Honour said it was quite clear that the plain-Aff had sued before the proper time and non-suited him.

A CARTaa's CLAlM—ltilatthew Thomas, carter, Run- corn, stied William Howard, also of Runcorn, for the sum of £4 151. 9d. for carting done.—The plaintiff stated that the account was due for carting materials to two houses which were built by the defendant in 1892. Be had seen him many times since and the de- fendant had promised to pay the account. —A receipt for the payment of £2 on account was preduced by the defendant, but the plaintiff denied having received the money,and said he was quite surprised when he saw the receipt. It was not his signature.—ln answer to his Flonour the plaintiff said his wife made the accounts out. Alter comparing the handwriting on the receipt and the account, he said there was very little doubt that she had received the £2, and he would deduct that amount from the claim. The remainder must be paid at the rate of 44. per month.

div.head: ,jOMING ELECTION.
div.p: THE ,jOMING ELECTION.

According to Mr. Balfour's statement in the House of Commons on Tuesday evening, Parliament is to be dis- solved next Monday, and the writs for the general elec- tion, will, it is expected, be issued the same evening. In a manifesto addressed to the friends of religious equality the Executive Committee of the Liberation Soci- ety say:that what has been accomplished in the expiring Parliament marks a distinct advance in the progress of their movement. They must continue to rsquire from all Liberal candidates distinct pledges in favour of oiB- - in both Wales and Scotland. Nor need there be any reservation of opinion on the question of disestablishment in England also, whatever course may be deemed prudent in exacting pledges from the candi- dates in particular localities. Pointed reference is made to the claims which are beingput forward by the Church party in the matter of education, and it is urged that the success of the Liberationist programme will greatly depend on the issue of the coming contest. It is stated by Mr. Sexton that he desires after sixteen years' assiduous attendance to withdraw from the Com- mons and not to offer himself as a candidate at the next election. Many of Mr. Sexton's colleagues are strongly urging him to reconsider the matter. At a meeting of Parnellites from all parts of Ireland held in Dublin on Tuesday it was decided to contest 24 out of the 32 Irish counties and all the borough seats, with the possible exceptions of Derry and Belfast. The Committee of the Irish Temperance League have issued an appeal to the people of Ireland, in which they remark that those engaged in the liquor trade speak of their business as one of the few flourishing Irish industries and claim that it should therefore be protected. "But surely," they add, "a , usiness that makes in Ireland in one year 90,000 men and women into drunkards has no right to claim consideration from patriots or protection from the State."

The National Education Association draws the atten- tion of the electors of the country to the proposal to further assist denominational schools out of the rates and taxes, and points out that the demands now made by the Established Church imply a further charge on the taxpayers of at least £2,000,000 a year. An address to the electors has been drawn up by the Special Consultative Council of the United Kingdom Alliance. It states that the nation is greatly indebted to the late Government for its attitude towards temper- ance reforms. Though the Local Veto Bill has not been passed, an immense impetus has been given to the tem- perance movement, and temperance reform has been brought fully and irrevocably within the range of practical politics. A grave responsibility therefore rests on the electors. They are clearly and definitely called upon to decide whether in the House of Commons about to be elected the power shall rest with those who desire to give the people the means of effectually defending themselves against the devastating liquor traffic, or with those who are determined to withhold this right from the people. It is therefore urged that it is not the party to which a candidate belongs but his personal convictions and pledges with respect to the veto that ought to determine the vote of the temperance elector. MR. GLADSTONE'S FAREWELL.

Mr. Gladstone's farewell to his constituents in Midlo- thian was conveyed in a letter read at the annual meet- ing of the Midlothian Liberal Association on Wednesday. After expressing his gratitude for the treatment he had received " during fifteen happy years," Mr. Gladstone went on to say that though in regard to public affairs many things are disputable, there are some which be- long to history, and which have passed out of the region of contention. It is, as he conceives, beyond question that the century now expiring has exhibited since the close of its first quarter a period of unexampled activity both in legislative and administrative changes, that these changes taken in the mass have been in the direc- tion of true and most beneficial progress, that both the condition and franchise of the people have made in rela- tion to the former state of things an extraordinary ad- vance, that of those reforms an overwhelming propor- tion have been effected by the direct action of the Liberal party or of statesmen, such as Peel and Canning, ready to meet odium and to forfeit power for the public good, and that in every one of fifteen Parliaments the people of Scotland have decisively expressed their convictions I in favour of this wise, temperate, and in every way re- markabls policy. MANIFESTO BY THE NATIONAL REFORM UNION. The Parliamentary Committee of the National Reform Union has issued the following manifesto : To the electors of Great Britain and Ireland. Fellow- countrymen,—Parliament has been dissolved, and only a small part of the legislative work entrusted to the Liberal Government by the constituencies in 1892 has been accomplished. The experience of the last three years demonstrates more clearly than ever that few de- mocratic reforms are obtainable so long as the present electoral and legislative machinery continues unre- formed. We therefore earnestly press upon the atten- tion of the electors the absolute necessity of insisting upon such changes being effected as will make it possible that the will of the people shall be fully and clearly as- certained and expressed at the polling booths,and,when so ascertained and expressed, that it shall be speedily and effectually realised in legislative enactments, unim- peded by the present cumbrous and obsolete rules of Parliamentary procedure and freed from the insolent op- position of irresponsible hereditary legislators. To this end three great reforms are necessary :1. Such an alterations of the laws relating to registration and the franchise as will enable all duly qualified citizens to acquire more easily, speedily, and without cost, one vote, and one vote only, for a representative in Parliament, and the democratiza- tion of Parliament by relieving candidates of the costs of elections and by payment of members. 2. A reform of the present rules of Parliamentary procedure, which lend themselves readily to wilful obstruction and delay, and the devolution of all purely local business to bodies elected by and representing only the localities concerned therein. 3. The abolition of the legislative power of the House of Lords. In the forthcoming election every Radical candidate should be asked to pledge himself to support these reforms, without which it is idle to hope that any of those popular measures can be secured on I which Radicals have so long been practically unanimous. These include Home Rule all round, beginning with Ire- land ; Disestablishment and Disendowment of all State Churches ; the granting to the people the power to con- trol the sale of intoxicating liquors in their own districts; the reform of the laws relating to the acquisition ,tenure, ' transfer, and sale of land, so that farmers may enjoy fair rents, fixity of tenure, and freedom of sale and cul- tivation ; the discontinuance of all grants and pensions out of public revenues, except in return for adequate services rendered to the community: the acceptance of the principles of international arbitration, ot the recognition of the rights of weaker races, and of a closer union among the English- speaking races of the world; the taxation of all land values, including all mine rents and mineral royalties ; the extension of the just and sound financial principles embodied in Sir William Bar- court's great Budget, of the assimillation for purposes of taxation of realty and personalty and of the graduation of taxation based upon ability to pay ; the economical administration of the revenue of the country, so that the money collected from the people may be expended wisely and to its full value ; greater freedom from central control of the administra- tion of the poor law, and a fuller recognition of the claims of the sick, the aged, and those in temporary dis- tress ; and a practical admission of the claims of labour as set forth by its accredited representatives such questions as the limitation of hours, full right of com- bination, compensation for injuries, and direct repre- sentation in Parliament. By the practical fusion of the two winks of the so-called Unionist party in a coalition Government all the forces of monopoly, privilege, and , reaction have combined to prevent the accomplishment of these and other reforms. Against these forces must be evoked the courage and moral strength of a free and self-governing people. The issues at this election are simple and direct. It lies with you, electors, to decide by your votes whether you will continue to allow your needs to be neglected, your aspirations scorned, and your will thwarted by others, or whether you will es- tablish your government on a truly democratic basis, and secure the power, as you undoubtedly already pos- sess the right to govern yourselves in your cwu interest and in ycur own way.—W. THE COMING GOLD BOOM. TUE NORTFI-WEST AUSTRALIAN GOLD- FIELDS, LTD.

The coming autumn, it is generally admitted, will see, in connection with West Australian gold mining, a repetition of the Kaffir boom, with this difference that it is certain to be more emphasized and last longer. One of the companies that will play an important role in the , movement is the North-West Australian Gold-fields, Limited. There are many reasons for this assertion, the , principal being that the concern is moderately capita- used, it owns the best properties on the Pilbarra-field, has a most influential Board of Directors, including Mr. A. F. Calvert, the well-known authority on the colony's aurilerous wealth, and, with the exception of the Con- solidated Gold Mines of West Australia, possesses the largest working capital of any Westralian gold-miniag combination. A further point in its favour is that this money was all subscribed privately by those intimately connected with the venture. It OWO6 the celebrated Breen's, Osborne's, and Geyer's leases in the Taiga Tai- ga district, on and around which some startling fads were made last year. Wood and water abound, and a great portion of the reef can be worked by tunnelling simply, thus saving much labour and cost. The shares are now changing hands at 305., and at the price 1.)-e about the best on the entire Westralian list. An im- mense quantity of quartz is at grass certain to yield from 5a3. to eczs. of gold to the ton, and as crushing will soon commence the shares are on the eve of a great rise. This is the class of security to buy and hold Mr a few months, in order to double or even treble the value of one's iniii•nipent.

The children assembled at the school at 1.15 p.m., and at 1.30 p.m. the parade of ehe princillal lames of the Village began, the school brass band leading the way. Afterwards the children as- sembled in the Penketh Park where the remaining time before tea was agreeably spent in swinging and other juvenile games. The seniors amused themselves by playing a cricket match —the sides chosen representing the " Married " and " Unmarried" states;.of the male teachers and young men of the Sunday School. Tea was partaken of at 4 o'clock. The good things provided foi the refreshment of the inner man disappeared with marvellous rapidity,and the ladies who were responsible for the preparation of tea must have had any doubts or misgivings which before possessed them speedily re- moved. The tables had been tastefully decorated with dowers, &c., and the young ladies of the select class presided. This part of the day's programme was voted a thorough success. After tea adjournment to the re- creation ground was the order. Here all kinds of games and contests were indulged in, the brass band agreeably livening up the proceedings at intervals. At 9 o'clock a return to the scbool was made, where sweetmeats and other goodies were distributed. A most happy and en- joyable day's proceedings terminated with the raising of hearty and often renewed cheers for those friends who had contributed in any way to the day's enjoyment. SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN S.B.—Number of scholars on books: 188 boys, 135 girls; average 230; number of teachers: 33 male, 8 female; ministers :Revs..J. Kirtlan, Owen Watkins, G. D. Mason, and J. Gunnell; superin- tendents: Messrs. W. Brough and S. Blythe. The scholars left the school preceded by the banner at nine o'clock, and then went via Hood-lane to a field adj fining Bewsey Hall kindly lent by Mr. J. Bennett. Dinner and tea was provided at the field at which a number of friends at down. The day was spent in football, cricket, arid various other games and an enjoyable day was brought to a termination by a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Ben- nett and family. BANK QUAY MISSION S S.—Number of scholars on books: 223 boys, 219 girls; average attendance : 195: boys, 185 girls; number of teachers :22 male, 14 female! president : Mr. N. Hough ; superinte dents:' Messrs. Joseph Monks and James Woolley. The scholars went in procession to Walton Lea where old English sports were held.

COCKIIEDGE MISSION S. S.—Number of scholars on books: 220 boys, 230 girls; average attendance : 140 boys, 130 girls; number of teachers : 12 male, 8 female ; number of books in library : 200; superintendents : Messrs. Plinston and H. Maybury. The scholars and teachers left school at 9.0 a.m.and went via :—Fennel-st., urch-st., Scotland-read, Horsemarket-st., Sankey-st , Bold-st.,Rylands-st., Bridge-st., thence to a field at back of Orford school,where dinner and tea were served to the children. Games were carried on through the day, and sports were held in the afternoon commencing at 2 p.m. The school breke up anout 8 p.m. The procession was headed by the Mission Band. ELLESMERE-STREET WESLEYAN MISSION S. S.—Number of scholars en books :120 boys, 182 girls; average attend- ance : 84 boys, 100 girls ; number of teachers: 12 male, 10 female ; number of books in library: 180 ; ministers: R •vs. J. Kirtlan, Owen Watkins and G. D. Mason ; sup- erintendent : Mr. Levi Richardson ; secretaries : Messrs. J. Lingard and W. Webb. The scholars met at school at 1 8.30, and the start was made at 9 o'clock. The proces- sion was preceded by a new banner, and the younger ' scholars were accommodated on lurr:es, two of which were provided by Mr. Howard, Hall-st., and one by Mr. Lent, Mersey-st. She procession passed up Buttermar- ket-st.and down Bridge-st.,the scholars proceeding direct to the field at Grappenhall, kindly lent by Mr. L. James. Dinner and tea were provided at the field and the day ryo9sed in the usual manner.

INDEPENDENT METHODISTS BRICK-STREET MISSION S. S. —Number of scholars on hooks : 186 boys, 200 girls ; average attendance : 140 boys, 181 girls ; number of teachers : 21 male, 26 female ; ministers : various ; superintendents ; Mr. James Shaw, Mr. W. Wright. A procession through the principal streets was formed, headed by the brass bind belongino to the school, after- wards going to the field kindly lent by Mr. Harris in Padgate-lime. The children were re,aled with beef sand- wiches for dinner, and curront and seed bread for tea, and an orange wis given to each child after tea. _

BUCKLEY-STREET S. S.—Number of scholars on books : 110 boys, 140 girls ; average attendance : 80 boys, 120 girls ; number of teachers : 7 male,B female ; ministers: Mr. Joseph Wibberley and others ; superintendents : Mr. William Hewitt,and Mr. John Adams. The scholars, teachers and workers met at 9 a.m. and formed pro- session numbering 300, headed by the brass band of the school under the leadership of Mr. J. Richardson. They took their usual route along Dallam-lane. Tanners-lane, Bewsey-street, Horsemarket-street, and Sankey-street, to the Park where they joined the main procession, arid folio :eel the main route until they reached Scotl ind- road, Buttermarket-street end, where they branched off and returned to the school where dinner was provided, consisting of Melton Mowbray Dies, ham and beef sand- wiches, to which ample justice was done by all. After dinner the scholars again formed procession, headed by the band and marched to a field in Orford-lane, kindly lent by Mr. Robinson, where the usual field games were indulged in such as cricket, football, sack-racing, three. leg race, blind races, etc. Very useful prizes made by the ladies ,ewing class were given to all the successful Gnes. At 5 o'clock the scholars, headed by the band were marched again to school for tea, consisting of ham and beef sandwiches, buns, arid other sweets. After tea was over the elder scholars and teachers went back to the field till dusk feeling justly satisfied with the day's enjoyment and looking forward to a fine day on the morrow for their annual picnic by bus to Alderley Edge. BAPTIST S. S. GOEDORNE•STREET.—Number of scholars on books 120 ; number of teachers : 11 male, 6 female ; superintendent : Mr. S. Fernley. A start was made at 8 o'clock in conveyances for Mr. Pimblotts' Barley Heyes who had kindly lent a field for the day. Varionsigames were indulged in and generally a most enjoyable day was spent a substantial dinner and tea was provided for scholars and officers. ACADEMY STREET MiSaIoN S. S.—Number of hcholars on books : 60 boys, 88 girls ; number of teachers : 10 male, 8 female ; minsters : various ; superintendents Messrs. Thomas Riley and Aquila Conk. The day's pro- gramme of this school consisted of a procession in com- pany with Friar's Green school through the town and thence to a field in Marsh Rouse-lane, kindly lent by Mr. Matthews in addition to allowing them the use of a large building. The day was afterwards spent in gmes,ericket, football and racing for useful articles. The children were served with meat pies and milk for dinner and buns and scones for tea. A refreshment bar was erected in the field, for the convenience of friends who might visit the field during the day. ST. PETER'S CHURCU S.S.—Number of scholars on books : 300 boys, 318 girls; average attendance : 240 boys, 250 girls ; number of teachers : 8 male,l2 female ; ministers: Rev. B. Percival, Rev. J. A. Cooil ;.superin- tendents: the clergy. Divine service was held at eleven o'clock, the preacher being the Vicar. The scholars assembled again at 1.30 and marched to a field at Padgate, kindly lent by Mr. Cox. There tea was served and various games indulged in, ST. ANN'S CHURCH S.S.—Number of scholars on books: 193 boys. 230 girls ; average attendance : 263 ; number of teachers : 10 male, 12 female ; mtnisters : the Rev. Jarn,S Davies and the Rev. Philip J. Bryne ; superinten. dents : 1-invS. Rey. J. Davies ; &rig, Miss N. Davies ; infants, Miss Downie ; secretary, Mr. Frank Taylor. The scholars and teachers sissembled at school at a quarter to nine, and proceeded to the Town Hall to join the main pron6asion, anti afterwards to the church. At three tea was held in the schools,and at four headed by the hand the scholars marched to a field (kindly lent by Mr. Wrigh*, farmer) in New-road, off Folly-lane. Here various amusements, including races, 141., for prizes were enjoyed, together with a pro- gramme of music by the C L.C. hand. Home. TRINITY CHURCH. S S —Nomher of scholars on books : 315; average attendance : 250; minister : Rev. E. C. E Carlton ; oecretary : Mr. Dunbehin. The scho- lars marched round the town with the general procession and afterwards svfmt to Frodshaen. • ST. PAUL'S CHURCH SS.—.'Number of scholars on hooka :250 boys, 450 girls ; ministers: Revs H. V. Pignt and E H. Townsend ; superintendents, Messrs. J. R. Lawless, and A. J. Jolley. After parading the town with the veneral procession, Service was held in the Church, and the scholars then pmeeded to a field in IV ildersoool. Over 230 prizes were distributed to the children on the field.

Sr. :jaws Cannat SS,—Nomber of scholars on brink. : 500 minigter., Rev.. F. Slater and E. superintendent, Mr. T. Gibann. After parading the town ar,d a service at the church, the schodirs nroceeded to a field in IVildrrponl near the Brewery, where the day was Tent in games, &c. At the procession the school was headed hy the bands of the Volunteers, and church Lads' Brigade. _ -
ORFORD CHURCH S.S.—Number of scholars on books: 56 boys : 66 girls; average attendance, 46 boys, 50 girls; number of teacb.rs, 2 male, 10 female; minister.

div.head: EX A
div.p: THE EX A

Rev. W. R. Hartwright ; superintendent, Rev. W. R. Hartwright. At 3 p.m. a shortened evensong with ad- dress was held at 3.30 p.m. ; procession through Orford was formed at 4.30 p.m. Tea was provided in the schoolroom followed by games, &c., in a field adjoining Orford Hall, kindly lent by Mrs. Beamont. ST. GEORGE'S CHURCH MISSION S.S.—Number of scholars on books: 180 boys, 240 girls; average attend- ance: 135 boys, 180 girls; number of teachers: 5 male, 18 female; number of books in library: 200; minister: Rev. G. B. Thurston ; superintendent: Rev. G. B. Thurs- ton. The scholars joined the procession at 9.30, after which they attended service at Parish Church at 11. Tea was provided at 4, and the day was spent in S. Elphin's Park. _ .

ST. LUKE'S CHURCH s.s.—Number of scholars on books: 220 boys, 230 girls; average attendance : boys, 8 ; girls, 400 ; number of teachers: 12 male, 14 female ; ministers: Rev. H. R. Wild,M.A. ; superintendent : Rev. H. R. Wild; secretary, Mr. T. Sutcliffe. The scholars assembled at two o'clock at S. Luke's schools, proceeded to a field adjoining Liverpool-road where games were indulged in. Tea was partaken of at five o'clock. Sr. BARNABAS S.S. —Number of scholars on books 275: minister: Rev. G. Allton ; superintendent: Mr. R. Y. Woollacott. The members of the school walked round the town headed by Messrs. Fletcher and Co.'s Gas Engineers Band, afterwards returning to church service 0111 where the preacher was the Rev. J. Llewellyn,late curate. Alter service, children went to their homes and re-assembled at two, proceeding to the field adjoining the schools, and here games of all kinds were indulged in and prizes, itc., were given. Tea was partaken of at four. The scholars dispersed at nine, each child being served with cake, buns, biscuits, &c. Every one was well attended to and made to enjoy themselves by their clergy and teachers. ALL SAINTS MISSION S. S.—Number of scholars on books : 150 boys, 250 girls ; average attendance morn- ing 200 afternoon 360 ; number of teachers : 6 mate,ll female,: ; minister : The Rev. H. V. Pigot ; superin- tendent ; Mr. Peter Sudlow. The scholars and teachers walked in procession along with St. Paul's. Tea was held in the school room after which the school joined with St. Paul's in a field by St. James' Church, Wilderspool- road.

- ST.MARYS R.C.S.S.BIITTERMARIKET-STREET. —Number of scholars on books: 366 b,)ys, 316 gir,s ; average attend- ance ; 342 boys, 287 girls ; number of teachers : 12 male 12 fema!e ; ministers : Rev. F. W. Sumner 0.5.13., Rev. M.E. Duggan,O.S.B.; superintendents, Mr. John Mallins, and Miss Jane Ramsay. The afternoon was, spent in a field at Orford.

ST. ALBANS R.C. S.S. BEWSEY•STRBET.—NUMber Of scholars on books : 135 boys, 143 girls ; average atten- dance : 120 boys, 121 girls ; number of teachers : 2 male 9 female; number of books in Library : 200 ; ministers : Revs. A. D. Firth, 0.5.., John S. Cody, o.S.B.,Thomas J. Craven' 0.5.8. ; superintendent : Mr. D. Morris. The scholars formed in procession and proceeded along Tanner's-lane, Winwick-st, Horsemarket-at., Bridge-st., Mersey-st., Buttermarkst-st„ Sankey-st., Legh-et,, and Bolleston-et., returning to the Church for Benediction. Tke order of procession was as follows :—Cross bearers and altar boys : Orford-lane school—infants, girls and boys ; King-st.school—infants,girls and boys;Children of Meryl; Mount Carmel confraternity; men's confraternity of the Sacred Heart. The scholar's tea was distributed in the field at Padgate, belonging to Mr. Norcott, at 4 p.m., and at the field a gala was held, at which there were sports, dancing, &c._ _ . _

_ WARRINGTON BAGGED S. S. AND MISSION.—Number of scholars on books: 180 boys, 220 girls ; average attend- anca : 110 boys, 140 girls : number of teachers : 8 male, 10 female ; superintendent : Mr. Tames Skelland, 115, Lovely-lane,Warrington ; essistant-superintendent : Mr. F. J. Owen, 2, Bramhall-street ; financial and general secretary : Mr. Edmund Osborne, 129, Lovely-lane ; school secretary : Mr. W. Sparks, 15, Guardian-street. The children met at the school, Be wsey-street, at 8.30 a.m., when each scholar was given a bun or scone. They afterwards got in order and marched in two's to the Town Hall and from thence in procession through the principal streets headed by the band of the school. They then adjourned to a field in Lovely-lane, kindly lend by Mr. Bennett, of Clap Gate Farm. Dinner con- sisting of pies, &c., was partaken of, and games, racing for prizes, &c. were indulged in until tea. The games were then ' resumed till 8 o'clock when the children dis- persed alter spending a happy day. The members of the sewing class have been very busy of late making frocks, &c., for the poorest children so that they can be happy for at least one day in the year. All the father- less and motherless children have been presented with a new pair of boots each. The committee wish to thank all the kind ladies, including Mrs. Hodgkinson, and Mrs. Poole' for the clothing, &3. which they have given them for the poor and destitute children. . . . .

_ BLUE COAT Serroor..—Number of scholars on books : 33 boys, 22 girls ; average attendance : 33 boys, 22 girls ; numh.r of teacher; : 3 mile ; number of books in library : 250 ; superintendent : Mr. Edward Rose. The procession was joined in the morning, alter which service was attended at the Parish Church. A visi;a,tion by friends and relatives of the scholar was made in the afternoon. Tea and sports on the grounds belonging to the school were indulged in, in the evening. PADGATE INDUSTRIAL SCHOOL. —Number of scholars on books: 100 boys, 68 girls ; number of teachers : 2 male, 1 female; number of books in library, 60 vols ' • minister, R-v. J. J. Langham ; superintendent : Mr.H. M. Mines. Children went by train from Padgate to Warrington at 8.55 a.m. They joined procession in the Park, and after- wards attended service in th=l Parish Church with other children. After service buns and milk were given to the children prior to their match home to Padgate. The band was in attendance and several guardians walked with the children in the procession. The afternoon was spent in a field at Woolston kindly placed at their dis- posal by Mr. Joseph W. Houghton, where various games and sports were indulged in during the remainder of the day. A good tea consisting of buns, sandwiches,and tea was served to the children on the field, after which they received a supply of nuts and oranges. WORKHOUSE.—Number of soholars on books : 22 boys, 28 girls ; teacher : Miss Ward ; ministers : Rev. H. V. Pigot and Rev. Father Ryan. LEGH ST. Pinturrivm METHODIST S.S.—The scholars marched in procession through the town and then adjourned to a field at Folly Farm, kindly lent by Mr. Wright.

div.head: WALKING DAY AT PENKETII.
div.p: WALKING DAY AT PENKETII.

The annual Sunday school scholar's treat was held on Friday at Penlieth. The St. Mary's Sunday school met at Sankey at 10 a.m.,and headed by the brass band marched down to the Mission room, whare the Penketh scholars were waiting for them. The Church Lad's Brigade mustered some 60 strong and presented a very military appearance, as they marched in front of the procession with their riflps at the slope. The smaller children were conveyed in carts, and the elder ones walked bearing the usual banners. The procession pro- ceeded to the Illack Horse, Sankey Bridges, and than re- turned to Sankey Sunday schools for lunch. Afterwards games were indulged in Mr. J. Fairclough's field, and sports in connection with the Brigade were held. Tea was provided at 5 p.m., and the remainder of the even- ing was pleasantly spent. The band played in the even- inv, for dancing.

WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.—The scholars met at the school at 1.30 pm., and headed by the baud, marched round the village. The weather was most unpropitious, rain falling very heavily. The procession proceeded to the Park and remained till tea time, and then a move was made to the Recreation Ground where races were indulged in and games played.

div.head: lIARRIAGE OF MISS SMITH OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: lIARRIAGE OF MISS SMITH OF WARRINGTON.

A marriage in which many people in Warrington were greatly interested,was solemnized between Mr.tieorge A. Macdonald, of 12 Manor-road,Sidcup,lient,and Winifred Mary, eldest daughter of Dr. T. S. Smith, F.R.C.S., of Warrington and Birkdale, at the Trinity Wesleyan Church,Southport,on Thursday afternoon last week. 'Fhe officiating clergyman was the Rev. F. W. Macdonald, father of the bridegroom. The bride who was given away by her father, was very tastefully attired in white silk brocade, ornamented with pearl embroidery, white heather, and orange blossoms, and she wore a Honiton lace veil which had been worn by her mother on the occasion of her marriage. The bridesmaids,Miss Dorothy and Miss Hilda Smith, sisters of the bride, and Miss Florence Macdonald, sister of the bridegroom, wore cos- tumes of white and primrose glace!, silk trimmed with chiffon and lace. They carried shower-bouquets of yellow roses and mignonette, and wore gold bracelets, the gifts of the bridegroom. Mr. Donald Macdonald fulfilled the duties of best man for his brother while Dr. Reginald Smith, the bride's eldest brother, presided at the organ and played the " Bridal March" from Lohengrin, and Mendelssohn's " Wedding March." Following the ceremony a reception was held at Dr. and Mrs. Starkey Smith's residence, St. Austin's, Birkdale. Later in the after- noon the newly-married pair left for the Lake District, where the honeymoon will be spent. The bride's travel- ling ccstume was a tailor-made gown of fawn-coloured cloth, with Tattersall vesting,and trimmed with guipure lace, and a straw hat trimmed with lilac. The weduing cake was supplied by Messrs. div.head: FRODS HAM.
div.p: FRODS HAM.

DEATH AND FUNERAL OF SERGEANT THOMAS.—OG Saturday afternoon there passed away at his residence at Frodsham Police Station, Sergeant William Thomas who has been stationed in the district for about two years. Prior to this he had occupied positions in the Cheshire Constabulary at Northwich, Marston, Dukin- field. Buglawton, and Hyde. tie had been a victim to inflaenza, having been attacked on four occasions, and a short time ago he broke a blood vessel. He had been ailing ever since, and his death although somewhat sud- den, was not unexpected. He leaves a widow but no famlly. He wag 34, years:of age. The funeral took place at Hyde on Tuesday.

div.head: DARESBURY.
div.p: DARESBURY.

PRESENTATION TO TEM OVERIiBER.---A number of the principal ratepayers of Newton-by-Daresbury assembled in the Board School on Friday evening, fcr the purpose of presenting Mr. Philip Darbyshire, on his retirement frotn the office of overseer after 45 years' service, with a valuable and elegant, nrmulu clock, ornamented with Sevres china, and supplied by Messrs. Elkington and Company. There were present—Captain Rodger, and Messrs Philip Darbrshire, E. Bretherton. D. Fowles, Thomas Priestley, Thomas; Billington, James Houghton, James Ryder, John Taylor, Szo. The clock bore the Fol- lowing inscription :—" Presented to Mr. Philip Darby- shire, by the ratepayers of Newton-by-Daresbury, on his resignation of the cffice of overseer after 45 years' ser- vice." Captain Rodger made the presentation. and said that on behalf of their fellow parishioners Ise ex- pressed his high appreciation of Mr. Darbyshire both as friend and neighbour. Few men had retained such a position—one which was often the cause of friction— and yet left it retaining the universal good-will of the community, as he had done. Wishing him still mans' I years of going in and out amongst them he begged of Darbyshire to accept this remembranceof them all." Mr. Darbyshire then briefly responded, stating his in- ability to adequately express his high appreciation of the good feeling extended towards him during the many years he had held office, and which had culminated in the purchase of an unexpected and valuable present, which would be highly prized as long as he lived to see it. A hearts. vote of thanks to Messrs. Heaton, Brether- ton, and D. Fowles, for soliciting subscriptions towards the presentation fund,was proposed by Mr. T. Priestley, and seconded by Captain Rodger, to which Mr. Brether- ton responded, assuring the meeting that both he and Mr. Fowles had had much pleasure in doing so. Mr. Fowles then proposed that a vote of thanks he given to Captain Rodger for making the presentation, and the easant meeting terminated.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 6, 1895

div.head: EARLESTOWN A.ND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN A.ND NEWTON.
DRUNKENNESS.

At the Town IlaiVisie-s-v—t-0.U.,—0-ii-Tuesday morning, before Mr. C. B. F. Borron, Maria Lennon, living in Robin's-row,llaydock,was charged with being drunk in Ilaydock-st., Earlestown, the previous evening. She was fined 28.64. and costs or 14 days.

GOOD TEMPLARS. The weekly meeting of the Hope of Earlestown lodge of Good Templars was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall, Earlestown, on Monday evening. Bro. W. Wilson C. T. presided,and there was a fair atten- dance of members. The digest of business for No.l Convention to be held at Leigh on Saturday week was read by Bro. Barker (secretary) and delegates were appointed. The meeting was afterwards de- clared open, and a number of friends were admitted Bro. G. Clarke presided and gave a short address. A good programme of songs recitations, and musical selections was given by Bro. W. Wilson, W. H. Crowther, H. Barker, IL Ambrose, and Sister F. Holliday. An address on "The unemployed," was given by Bro. E. Boreland and intently listened to. At the close thanks were tendered to the speaker. CADETS OF TEMPERANCE PIC-N1C....

--- The annual pic-nic in connection with the Samuel Morley Sectionof the Cadets of Temperance took place on Saturday afternoon. The weather was very threatening, and not at all propitious for an outing of this character; The children number- ing about 100 mustered at the Co-operative Hall, at one o'clock, and after being marshalled in proces- sion, proceeded through one or two of the streets to the station, where they took the 1.34 train for Lea Green. On arrival there they proceeded to Mickle- head Green,to a field kindly placed at their disposal by Mr. G. W. Rawlins, where they enjoyed them- selves in various ways until tea time. After tea the children amused themselves in racing and other games until 8.30, when they made their way to the station and left for Earlestown by the 9.7 train and reached home without mishap. WESLEYAN CHOIR PICNIC.

The members of the choir attached to the Wes- leyan Church, Earlestown, had their annual picnic to Llandudno, en Saturday. The party numbering 22. including the Rev. J. Bartley, 'Astor, left Earles- town at 7 o'clock, and reached Llandudno about 10.30. The morning was pleasantly spent in stroll- ing on the promenade, the music played by the splendid band in the pavilion being very much en- joyed. Dinner was partaken of at the Grosvenor restaurant, and being well served was thoroughly enjoyed. In the afternoon the party set out for a drive in the direction of Colwyn Bay, and on re- turning several of them went round the Great °rose's Head. Tea was partaken of at the Grosvenor and a start for home was made at 6.50, Earlestown being reached shortly before 10 o'clock. The day was very fine and the out was thoroughly enjoyed. EARLESTOWII WOMEN'S LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. A meeting of this Association was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, on Monday after- noon. Mrs. G. W. Rawlins presided, and she was supported by Mrs. Moon (wife of the candidate). and a large number of ladies. Mrs. Rawlins ex- plained why they had been called togethar,pointing out that in view of the near approach of a general election it was necessary that the women should assist to return a Liberal member, and after detail- ing in what manner they could assist, impressed upon them the desirability of beginning at once. After discussing the various plans proposed in con- nection with the election, an executive committee was appointed, which it is understood will be able to assist materially in various ways the fight Mr. Moon is engaged in. Committee rooms have been engaged near the Wesleyan School, and any assist- ance which Liberals feel they can render will be gratefully accepted. NEWTON DIVISION CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATION. A special meeting of the Council of this associa- tion was held at the Town Hall, Newton, on Satur- day afternoon. Mr. T. D. Grimke-Drayton, vice- chairman of the Council, presided in the absence of Mr. T. H. Pearson, who is at present unwell, and amongstithose present were Colonel It. Pilkington, Colonel J. L. Wood, Messrs. T. J. Gillespie, C. B. F. Borron, W. Valiant, Wyndham Smith, W. Holland Owen, C. F. Clarke, J. E. Pardey, J. Robinson,Jonas Forster. A. Sutton, W. Lamb, &c. The meeting was called for the purpose of thanking the Hon. T. W. Legh, M.P., for his past services, and to request him to become the Unionist candidate at the ensu- ing election. A resolution to this effect was pro- posed by Mr. W. Valiant, and seconded by Colonel Pilkington, and carried. Mr. Legh, who was wait- ing in an ante-room was informed of the decision of the Council, and escorted into the hall, where he was received with much cheering. Mr. Legh, in I response to the invitation, thanked the Council for the kind expression of confidence, and intimated his willihgness to represent the Unionist cause at the coming election. CONSERVATIVE Pic NIC FROM EARLESTOWN. The annual pic-nic in connection with the Newton and Earlestown Polling District Conserva- tive Club took place on Saturday. Through the kindness of Lord Derby, Knowsley Park was placed at their disposal for the afternoon. Wagonettes were chartered to convey the party, numbering 200 members and friends to their destination. The weather was somewhat unfavourable for the out- ward drive, heavy showers falling at intervals, but little inconvenience was experienced in this respect during their sojourn in the Park. The Viaduct Works brass band accompanied the pic-nic, and lively selections of music were discoursed en route. On arrival a pleasant ramble round the Hall and gardens was much enjoyed, the party afterwards partaking of a substantial tea in a capacious tent erected in the park. Mr. Berry of the Wellington Inn, Prescot, had charge of the catering, which was very satisfactory. Alter the meal the hand played for dancing, while considerable amusement was derived from the foot races which took placr The 120 yards handicap was won by P. Shaw, J. Kynas- ton being second. Handicap for men over 30 years old, IT. Bowes, 2, C. Chorlton. The ladies race was won by Mrs. Cookson. Three leg race; I. Messrs. T. Siddeley and J. Kynaston, 2, T. Bowes and S. Appleton. Committee's race, 1, J. Kynaston, 2, T . Siddeley. The drive for home was commenced at 17.45, Earlestown being reached about 10 o'clock. ' The arrangements made by the Committee were of an excellent character. 1.0.G.T. EARLESTOWN EBENEZER LODGE. No. 752.

The Lodge held their usual weekly session on Tues- day in the Co-operative Hall. After the usual busi- ness had been done, the programme was proceeded with. Songs were given by Bros. J. Singleton,who was responsible for the night, Bros. W. J. Taylor and W. Crowther, and Sisters Foster and Whitty. Bro. J. Taylor gave a very interesting Lancashire reading, after which the Lodge closed in due form, and the members adjourned to the shop of Mr. Smith and had refreshments at the married mem- bers' expense._

div.head: SONS OF TEMPERANCE.
div.p: SONS OF TEMPERANCE.

On Saturday last the members of the Samuel Morley Section of Cadets of Temperance held their annual picnic and tea. The members met at one o'clock at the Co-operative Hall and marched in procession to the station, the route being Welling- ton and Market-streets, the members,wearing their badge, being in charge of the following officers :-- Bro. J. Judson, W. Wheatley, J. Pickett. J. French, D. Robinson, W. Pearson, and proceeded in special carriages attached to the 1.34 train to Lea Green. On alighting, the procession was reformed and marched to Micklehead Green School and field. which was kindly placed at their disposal for the day, free of charge by Messrs. Rawlins. On arrival the members soon were busy with the swings and merry-go-rounds. cricket, &c., the adult friends dispersed for a ramble to view the country round. Tea was served in the schoolroom when 100 cadets and 50 friends sat down to an excellent tea provided by the following ladies :—Mesdames Judson, Pearson, Bars, Barrett, Reece, Clare, Ilipwood, an Porter,to which ample justice was done, after which various games and races were enjoyed by the youngsters who returned homewards by the 930 train, all pleased and tired. The thanks of the Section were presented to Bro. Thomas Molyneux for his gifts of nuts and other things for the children, also to Messrs. Rawlins for school and field. The provi- sions, which were of an excellent character, were supplied by Bro.T Molyneux. On Wednesday even- ing the Section met in the Co-operative Hall at 7 o'el wk. Worthy Patron presided. The officers for the present term were W.A. Ethel Pearson,V.A. Arthur Smith, G. Arthur Porter, and W. Alfred Cronin. Two new members were initiated. A visit was paid by Bro. W. Burrow., G.W.P. Bro. E. Andorton, G.W.C. Bro. G. Burrows, of Sr. Helens. At 8 o'clock the Britain Need Divi- sion snet the O.W p., Bro. Burrows presided, and installed the officers. Several of the members ex- pressed their pleasure with the Cadets' picnic on Saturday.

An authority tells ns that during the twat peaceful years the world has 3.700.000 soldiers, who are with- drawn from productive occupations to pose ps soldiers. The nay, equipments, food, and clothing of these men cost the world's taxpayers nearly £1,690,000 a day.

div.head: NEWTON DIVISION.
div.p: THE NEWTON DIVISION.
MR. JAMES MOON ADOPTED AS THE LIBERAL
CANDIDATE.

With enthusiastic unanimity, Mr. James Moon was adopted as the Liberal candidate for the division at a meeting of the Liberal Three Hundred of the Newton Parliamentary Division of the Sonth-West Lancashire held on Saturday evening, in Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, and presided over by Mr. Gerald W. Raw- lins, chairman of the Liberal Association of the division. For several months past Mr. Moon has periodically visited various districts in the division, and on each occasion,whether engaged addressing a public audiences or moving in and out among the electors individually,he has invariably been most cordially received. Indeed,so hearty and spontaneous has been the welcome extended to him amongst all classes and ranks in the division,that despite the fact of the constituency at present and for a long time past being represented by a Con servative member, the Liberal party has regained hope of the seat being won, and believe that with Mr. Moon as their candidate at the approaching election, they will be able to reverse the decision at the last Par- liamentary contest, when the Hon. T. W. Leg,,h, son of Lord Newton, the local landowner, was triumphant by a margin of 890—the largest majority the Tories have ever recorded in the division. This faith oft e Liberals is in some degree based on the knowledge that hitkerto anything like real organisation in the rank and file of their party has been lamentably conspicuous by its ab- sence. Since the last election there has been a large in- crease of population in the division, a circumstance which leads to a reasonable assumption that the present position of the two political parties is aa unknown quantity. Should this assumption prove to be well ieunded, the result will depend very largely on the ' amount of work put into the election by the respective ' parties. A few words about the Liberal candidate may net here be out of place. Mr. Moon is thirty-seven years of age, having been born in Preston in the year 1858. His • school life was spent at Birkenhead and Southport,at the • late Mr. Templar's academy. In his sixteenth year he was apprenticed to a firm of timber merchants and cabinet makers,and for three years worked at the bench to learn the trade. At the expiration of that time he , joined his brother in the assurance business, in which he , has been engaged ever since. During his business career ; he has worked himself up step by step until he now , holds the very responsible position of chief in Liverpool .• of the Prudential Assurance Company. Be hae won , troops of good friends amongst the large staff of the ' company, with whom he has been brought into constant contact. As a Wesleyan Mr. Moon is well know n,having , filled all the offices open to laymen. Be was a lay mem- , bar of the last Wesleyan Conference. The Liverpool Reform Club Committee claims him as a member, and he is also an associate of the Institute of Actuaries. His • Liberalism is sound and consistent,as his addresses from time to time show Necessarily, by reason of his busi- ness connections, Mr. Moon hag had an extensive and varied experience of the working classes, and is pecu- liarly well adapted for dealing with such a question, for instance, as that of old age pensions. Personally he is , sanguine of wresting the honours of representation from the present holder, granted of course that the full Libe- ral reseurces of the division are at his back. _ .

_ The meeting of the Liberal Three Hundred of the divi- sion on Saturday evening was throughout characterised by a warmth of feeling towards Mr. Moon most marked and significant. As already conveyed, Mr. Rawlins pre- sided, and in a few prefatory remarks alluded to the current political crisis. With regard to Mr. Moon, he said it would have been impossible for the Liberals of that division to find a better man as their candidate. His sturdy Liberalism would vindicate itself. (Hear, hear). Mr. Moon then addressed the meeting. No doubt all had been looking forward to that meeting with great interest, but he questioned whether any realised a week ago that they would so soon be on the warpath in the struggle to win Newton for the Liberal party. Person- ally, he left himself with the greatest confidence in the hand.; of that meeting. If they did him the honour of selecting him as their candidate, he was prepared to fight their battle to the utmost extent of his power. It was a matter of the greatest satisfaction to him that he did not come before them as a total stranger. He had had the privilege of addressing Liberals in many parts of the division, so that they had had time to form their opinions, and by those opinions he was quite prepared to abide. He did not profess to be infallible, neither was he omnipotent or omniscient any more than his hearers, but he claimed to be a sound Radical, in thorough sympathy with the true spirit of Radicalism of which the late Gevernment had undoubtedly given proof. (Applause.) The principles enunciated in the Newcastle programme were the ones on which he asked for support. At the head of that programme stood first and foremost the question of self-government or Home Rule for Ireland. They were told it was on that question the Unionists had sacrificed themselves ; but he solemnly believed that in this question, as in others, the Conservative party was quite prepared to steal the clothes of the Liberals. (Applause.) After the efforts the Liberal party had put forth, it could claim the hearty and en- thusiastic support of every Irishman in the division who believed in Home Rule. (Applause.) The question of the House of Lords was one which the late Govern- ment had undoubtedly made a burning one. The House of Lords had used its powers to oppose Liberal legisla- tion for years, and was to-day simply a branch of the Carlton Club. Even Conservatives admitted that it les quired reform. The hereditary principle was a degrad- ing one, and he was in favour of ending it once and for all. (Applause.) He (the speaker) was in favour of Welsh diseatablishment as much as Mr.Ghamberlain was when he said, "I am a Noncnnformiet,born and bred in Dissent, and am opposed from honest convictions to anything in the nature of the State interfering with religion." (Applause.) The Welsh Church could not be defended, and, considering that the whole, of the endowments for the last 200 rears were being kept by the Welsh Church,the charge about robbery was untrue, lie was not one who believed that people could he made happy by Arts of Parliament, but by social legislation they could he a good deal by the well-being of the country. He was convinced that the liquor traffic, and especially the tied-house system, was at the root of eold deal of the poverty and misery which prevailed to such a deplorable extent. He greatly regretted that temperance should boa party question, and that the reasonable Bill which the late Government brought in was not passed. (Applause.) Ha believed the longer the settlement 01 this question was delayed the wone it would be for the trade. He would support any Bill brought in on the eame lines as that of the late Govern- ment. Another matter of the utmost importance was the Present state of the land laws, which were framed by the I .ndlord classes of the past in the interest of the landlord. They now had the result in land being uncul- tivated and permits being driven from it to the towns. evercrowding the labour markets there and reducing the wages. He would support a land bill like that brought in by Mr. Lambert, enabling a tenant to claim compen- sation for all improvements, and making it impossible for a landlord to reap the benefit on money scent by his tenant. RP would support compensation for disturbance without a proper reason (applause). What, they wanted SCAR to cheapen the transfer of land, to abo- lish entail, and give power to local authorities to acquire land at a fair price. (Applause.) He believed in the principle of taxing land kept out of nee at its fair value. At present a piece of land worth £l,OOO, and increasing its value Yearly if unoccupied, escaped taxation, and oftentimes was kept out of use however much it might be needed by the people. He would support a bill to remedy that. Closely allied to the land question Was that of mining and coal royalties, which would have to he dealt with sooner or later in the interests of the colic' try. NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of this Council was held on Monday, at the Earlestown Town Hall. Mr. C. B. F. Borron, J.P., C.C., presided, and there were also pre- sent Messrs. W. Collingwood, P.MacMahon, W.Uilmour, J. Simpson, J. Smith, J.P., W. Thompson, jun., J. W. Emmett, J.P., J. Slee, W. Beatty, T. Ormand, E. T. Evans, F. J. Wood, Rev. E. W. W. Kaye, J. E. Worsley (law clerk), and R. Brierley (clerk and surveyor). HIGHWAYS, &C., COMMITTRE. The minutes of this committee which were pub- lished in our last issue, were passed unanimously,on the motion of Mr. Collingwood, seconded by Mr. Mac- Mahon.
OAS AND WATER COMMITTEE,-ALLEGED TOO SHORT NOTICE TO MEMBERS.

Mr. J. Smith in moving the adoption of the minutes of this committee, said that be would state why the committee after being adjourned was called again on Wednesday, June 15th, to consider the tenders for coal. As he was leaving the Council chamber, it occurred to him that it would only be fair to the people who had contracted for coal to settle the question at the earliest possible moment, and he therefore took moon himself the responsibility of calling the meeting at 2.30 on Wednesday, June 19. He took upon himself all the responsibility of this action.—Mr. Thompson seconded the adoptien of the minutes.—Mr.Gilmour said that he attended the meeting on June 19th at great inconveni- ence to himself. He contended that it was not right that there should be so little notice given of the committee meeting. The notices were only sent out the same morning that the meeting was held. The chairman of the Gas and Water Com- mittee had distinctly told them that there was no hurry in the matter as there was sufficient coal to last until August. He also thought that the tenders should not have been considered when there was such a small at- tendance of the Committee present—only just a quorum. —Mr. Ormand said that he was not able to attend that meeting as he had unfortunately no knowledge of it. He left his house in the morning before the notice came, and did not get home until night, after the meeting was over. He also wished to know whether it was true that those whose tenders had been accepted had been in- formed of it prior to the confirmation by the Council. He would also like to know what were the prices of the tenders accepted.—Mr. Smith in reply said that with reference to calling the meeting, he considered that the persons who tndered for the coal should have an oppor- tunity of tendering somewhere else if not successful with them. Hence his calling the meeting as early as pos- sible. The persons who had been successful, were in- formed by the Surveyor that their tenders had been accepted subject to the approval of the Council. With reference to the prices he did not think it desirable that they should be published. He would however give them to the Council, but they were not for publication. Mr. Smith then read the prices which bad been accepted and said that they were considerably lower than last year.— Mr. Evans: If the coal is less, cannot you lower the price of gas ?—Mr. Smith: I cannot promise that. We have some of the old stock to use up yet. —The minutes were then confirmed.

FINANCE AND SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEES. The minutes of these committees which appeared in our last issue were passed unanimously, the former on the motion of Mr. Ormand. seconded by, Mr. MacMahon, and the latter on the motion of Mr. Borron, seconded by Mr. MacMahon. TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION COMMITTEE.

The minutes of this committee which appeared in our last issue were passed by a large majority, only Messrs. Emmett, Gilmour, Evans, and Ormand, voting against. No reason was given for their opposition.

div.head: PAVING OF BTRBEF3.
div.p: PAVING OF BTRBEF3.

In accordance 'with notice given Mr. Collingwood moved " That all resolutions of the Newton Improve- ment Commissioners or of this Council, relating to the paving of the private streets of the district with sets,be, awl are hereby, rescinded, and that the recommendation of the said committee as to the making of the following streets with macadam at the cost of the property owners be adopted :-.-Mercer-et., Walmsley-st.,Stanley- st., Raglan-st., Alpine-st.i Peel-st., Haydock-st., Water- st., (part of) Bradley-road, Birley-st.—Mr. Thompson seconded —Mr. Gilmour complained that Nelson-st., was not in this list,although its state was very bad.—lt was explained that there were difficulties in the way of it at present, but as soon as it was possible, the street would be naved.—The motion was then passed by a large majority, Messrs. Collingwood, MacMahon, Simpson, Smith, Thomnson, Slee, Kaye, Beatty, and Evans vot- ing for, and Messrs. Emmett, Gilmour, and Ormand, against.

THE APPOINTMENT OF OVERSEERS. Mr. Gilmour moved the resolution of which he had given notice : "That the Council consider their actual position relative to the appointment of overseers, seeing that the Law Clerk's opinion as to the number we are entitled to applint is at variance with that of the Local Gwernment Board, he having stated that we cannot anpoint more than two, whereas the Local Government Board say" not less than two nor more than four." He said that he had no personal feeling in the matter. But their law clerk said that the Council could only appoint two and nn more. He however knew of other places where they appointed three and four. He also saw by the memorandum from the Local Government Board that Councils could appoint not less than two nor more than four. He moved the resolution not from any feel- ing againat the Law Clerk, but he thought they ought to be guided right by their officers.—Mr. Emmett second ‘d the resolution, and thought that the law clerk should have an opportunity to correct himself in the matter.—Mr. McMahon also supported the motion. He said that the law clerk when questioned in March had said distinctly that not more than two could be ap- nointed.—Mr. Smith said that he did not think it necessary that the resolution should be putl to the meeting, as it was a question. It would be sufficient that the law clerk answer it.— This was agreed ta and the law clerk in reply said that he most honestly say that he had done all he could pre- vi, ugly to avoid answering Mr. Gilmour when he had brought up tho subject. He had done so because the question of the validity of the appointment of overseers involved the question of the validity of the poor rate upon which all the other rates were based. They ought to be extremely careful to guard that, especially as it was the first appointment by the Council. The memorandum of the Local Government Board, he had seen,and that certainly said that four could he appointed, • but it also recom- mended that the same number as heretofore should be appointed unless there were reasons for doing otherwise. The district previously only appointed two, and had he to advise the Council again, he would give the same advice that he gave in March.—Mr. Emmett and Mr. MacMahon said that they ought to know definitely the law in the matter.—The -law clerk said that they ought to be careful not to invalidate the appointment of overseers. There ought to be good reasons given before the number was raised to four.
RE-APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER. Th. Chairman cave notice that at the next meeting he would move the re-appointment of Dr. Watkins as me Beal officer of health.

THE DATE OF THE NEXT MEETING. The date of the next meeting falling on Bank Holiday, it was decided 4m the motion of Mr. MacMahon, seconded by Mr. Thompson to meet on the second Mon- day in Minot, e four o'clock. This concluded the business.

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.

A FTAYDOCR WOUNDING CASE.--At the Warrington Occasional Court, on Monday, before Mr. James Tinsley, Patrick Bigoina was charged with having on the 22nd June, at Havdnek, unlawfully and maliciously inflicted upon Frank Jackson certain grievous bodily harm. Frank Jackson, signalman, and employed by Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., Haydeck, and residing at Church-road. ilavdock. said that at about six p.m. on Sstupiay..Tune 22nd, he went for a walk, in company with Robert Jones, from Haydnck to Ashton. They returned together at about nine o'clock in the evening. They came along the footpath acrom the fields, through the Otd Boston yard. The prisoner and another man name on and passed them going in the same direction. The Prisoner asked "What have you got to say about me, Frank ?" Complainant di el not reply, but went on, and when he had got to the far side of the colliery yard the prisoner came up to him and hit him on the right side of the jaw. it was a very.hard blow, and it knocked him to the ground. Prisoner knelt on his back and hit him again with his fist on the face and head, ”ri afterwards kicked him several times about the head. He becaine unconscious, and when he recovered be put hi a hand on the ton of his head and found a hole from which blood was flowing. He got up and hurried away as quickly as he could. Meeting P.C. Blackburn he made a statement to him, and he took him home,bathed his head, nut a bandage on, and took him to Dr. Hay- ward's surgery, where he saw Dr. Hayward and Dr. Rnsliter, Dr. Hayward'a assistant. The two doctors dressed his wounds. The next morning he went into the Haviock Cottage Hospital. He had come from that institution that morning, was going hack again, and was under the care of Dr. Rossiter. Robert Jones gave corroborative evidence. Dr. Rossiter gave evineneeas to the wounds he found on Jackson's head. P.C. Blackburn said when he arrested prisoner he replied, "I thumped him, butt did not kick him." The prisoner, who now said " lAo not wish to say anything, and I have no witnesses to call," was committed to the Liver- pool Quarter Sessions for trial. He was not admitted to bail.

What annears to have been a most brutal murder o a child took place at VValthamstow on Saturday niebtf Florrie Ttobah, the six•year-nld claurzhter of a driver,wa, sent out for some beer. She did not return, and a subs sequent search for her proved unavailing. On Sunday. her body was found concealed at a considerable distance from the public-house to which the child had been sent. A medical examination showed that a dreadful crime had been committed.

div.head: INTERNAIIONAL RAILWAY CONGRESS.
div.p: INTERNAIIONAL RAILWAY CONGRESS.
VIM TO tARLESTOW.N.

Friday in last week was a red letter day at Earles- town, at least so far as the Viaduct Works was con- cerned,consequent upon the honour done to the town by the visit of several members of the liiternational Rail- way Congress who as many will be aware, are visiting the great railway centres in England. The party which visited Earlestown comprised a portion of those who had visited Liverpool the previous day, and they were conveyed direct from Edge Hill in a special train made up of 11 splendid dining saloons. Great preparations had been made in anticipation of the visit, and every- body was eager for a glimpse of the distinguished visi- tors. The special drew into Earlestown punctually at 10.50, the time set down for its arrival, and the Viaduct Works engine being attached to the rear end, the train was drawn up into the works, where the passengers alighted, every convenience being provided by Mr. J. W. Emmett for their comfort. When all had alighted it was found that about 50 had availed themselves of the opportunity of visiting Earlestown, the delegates, who represented France, Austria, Hungary, Italy, Ger- many, Spain, Belgium, Mexico, Finland, and North and South America,were accompanied by Hon. A.H.Holland- Hibbert and Mr. Ralph Broeklebank (directors of the company), Mr. F. Harrison (general manager), Mr. F. Ree (chiet goods manager), Mr.J.Shaw (superintendent, Lime-st.), Mr.J. W.Fletcher (telegraph superintendent), Mr. R. Turnbull (assistant superintendent of the line), and other officials of the company with interpreters. Having been introduced to Mr. J. W. Emmett, the delegates were placed under the conductorship of that gentleman, Messrs. C. W. and F. J. Emmett, .T. Barr, T. Ormand, and R. King and proceeded to inspect the various processes adopted in the manufacture of the goods rolling stock of the company. Everything of interest was fully explained,and copious notes,evidently for comparison, were taken by many of the delegates, who appeared greatly interested in what they saw. After inspecting the works the party proceeded to the Insti- tute recreation grounds, where they were photographed by Mr. T. Unsworth, of Earlestown. They afterwards adjourned to the large reading room for lunch. The room bad been previously decorated in an artistic man- ner, and presented a really gay and festive appearance, the decorations having been carried out under the super- vision of Mr. C. W. Emmett. During lunch,which was presided over by Mr. Ralph Brocklebank, the works band, stationed in the grounds outside, played the German, French, and American National Anthems, and "Rule Britannia." After lunch, the Chairman,speaking on behalf of the Chairman ofathe Company and his col- leagues, said he had to express the great pleasure it gave him to see the members of the Con- gress there that day. They appreciated very much the honour the distinguished gentleman present had conferred on the company by coming there. The Company were extremely anxious that the delegates should not leave the country, before they had seen, not only the locomotive works, where they constructed the power for drawing the trains, but also the wagon works where they constructed the wagons,and on the next day those who were able would go and see how they con- structed the carriages. The Company maintained for themselves that they built the best wagons in the coun- try, and as cheaply as possible, and that they had an excellent staff of people in every department. and in ad- dition, they did all the work on the premises. He was quite certain that the interchange of opinions and views between one country with another in these matters could only be to the advantage of all persons concerned. (Ap- plause). Ere then proposed the health of the "Queen ' which was enthusiastically honoured. Herr Ludwig (chairman of the Hungarian State Railways) replied in French, and concluded by proposing the health of the General Manager (Mr. F. Harrison), and the Superin- tendent of the works (Mr. J. W. Emmett). Mr. Emmett said he was highly pleased to have their visit there that day ; he thought it conferred a very great favour upon the wagon department. He could only say if they had been pleased in going through the works, it had been a great pleasure to him to conduct them. He thanked them most heartily for coupling his name with the toast. (Applause). Mr. Harrison also thanked them for the toast. He said he was not an expert in the management of such works, but to his mind tho wagon works was one of the best that could be found for neatness and economy. (Applause.) The party soon afterwards left and proceeded by the special train to London.

The 3rd and 4th King's Liverpool Regiments of Militia assembled at the Barracks of Orford on Monday morning, and in the afternoon left by special trains at four and five o'clock from Bank Quay Station for Altcar, where they will be en- camped for 21 days. The men, who numbered about 800, were under the command of Colonel C. C. Woodward, and the other officero who were with them included Major W. H. Hand, and Captains Beaman, Reddy and H. G. Walker. On Monday ait-e-in-oon-t-h-e- scholars it-,i-ending the Moore Wesleyan Sunday School had their annual treat. At 1.50 the juveniles, each carrying a bunch of flowers, assembled in the school, and after prayers had been said a procession was formed through the village, calling at several houses,where hymns were sung. A halt was made at the resi- dence of Mr. Sloane, and here refreshments were handed round to all present, to their evident en- joyment. Mrs. Forster kindly placed a field at their disposal, where games of every description were freely indulged in until four o'clock, when an ex- cellent tea was provide. The elder girls and Parents had tea provided for them in the chapel at five. The rest of the evening, until about nine, was taken up with races and sports of all kinds suitable to the tastes of the children, and before leaving oranges and buns were distributed. _ _

A BOOKFOR MARRIED WOMEN. The information contained in this book ought to be known by every married woman, and it will not harm the unmarried to read. The book is conveniently divided into 12 chapters. The first chapter treats of the changes at puberty, or when a girl becomes a woman. The second chapter treats of marriage from a doctor's standpoint ; points out tha best age for marriage, and who should have children and who not, and furnishes useful information that one can ordinarily get only , from an intelligent doctor. The third chlpter treats of the marriage of blood relations; and condemns such marriages as a rule. Chapter four treats of the signs of pregnancy. The fifth chapter tells how a woman should live during the pregnant state. The sixth chapter treats of mishaps and how to avoid them. The seventh chapter treats of maternal Impressions and shows that birthmarks are not due to longings in the part of the mother, bat rather to her poor health. The eighth chapter teaches how to have easy confinements. Certain people believe that women should bring forth in pain and trouble, but the hygienic physician says that confinements can be made comparatively easy i certain rules are obeyed ; these rules are given. The ninth chapter treats of the proper management of confinemen until the baby is born. The tenth chapter tells how to treat the mother till she is up and about again. The eleventh chapter treats of sterility ; Rives the main causes of it, how these may be overcome and children result The last chapter treats of the "change," a most important article for at women over forty. The book is full of useful information and no book is written which goes so thoroughly into mitten relating to married women. Some may think too much is told ; such can scarcely be the cave. for knowledge is power and the means of attaining happiness. The book can be had from Dr. T. R. SENSATIONAL SUICIDE. A MAN SHOOTS HIMSELF IN A RAILWAY CARRIAGE. As a ticket collector at the Central 'Station, War- rington, approached one of the compartments of the 10.30 a.m.express from Liverpool on ThursdaT,week for the purpose of collecting the tickets.he noticed a quantity of blood on the step, and on opening the carriage door he was horrified to find a man lying 1 against the window dead, and with a revolver in his hand from which he had fired two shots which had made a large wound in the temple. The deceased man was at once taken out of the carriage to a waiting-room, and afterwards to the Rams Head, Horsemarket-street. on Friday afternoon, it was discovered that the deceased was named John McCleary, and that he was a second officer of a steamer. TFIE INQUEST. The inquest was held at the Rain's Head, on Friday afternoon, by Mr. S. Brighouse. Mr. Simpson was present on behalf of the C.L.C. The first witness was John Milligan, Caroline Place, Ca 8 l 1 auot m t on c, near Birkenhead who identified the deceased Cleary, who resided with his aunt at Ventnor Place, Sharrow, Sheffield. He had no relatives except this aunt, whom he called "mother." He was second afficer on a steamer, but previously he had only been third officer. He was just about to take his first position as second officer. He was 25 years of age last Februarv• Witness last saw deceased alive at his (witness's) resid- ence in Claughton, on Thursday between 8 and 8.30 when he had his breakfast. Deceased was no relation to him, but was a friend. Deceased left his house at nine o'clock and went to a ship broker's office somewhere about ten o'clock, and when he left he promised to come to his (witness's', office, bnt he never came. When wit- ness got home about 8.30 p.m., he saw an account of the affair in the "Echo," and the account greatly upset him. Deceased was going to join a ship at Manchester which was outward bound, but stram.'e to say he had not taken his luggage with him, hiving left all his effects at Birkenhead. He had never said anything to lead any one to suspect that he would take away his life. He wanted to pass the examination for first officer. but he could not at present, as he had not done night watch, arid this appeared to worry him. fle had not however worried enough about it to cause any alarm. Witness had got him the berth to which he was going. He could give no reason why the act had been committed. There were marks on deceased's left arm, and these were caused by his attempting to take away his life with a razor about five years ago. He had never said why he had done that, but witness supposed that he was fattier- leas and motherless, and had no interest in ale wend. Witness had neverseen the revolver or cartridges before, and deceased must have bought them on the way to the station. Edward Hughes, foreman porter on the Central Station, said that on going to the compartment in which deceased was lie saw blood on the step, and on opening, he saw the floor of the compartment " swim- ming"with blood,whlch was also running not under the door. Deceased had evidently been dead some minutes, as the wound had stcpped bleeding. P.C. Millington said that he examined the clothing of deceased, and found in addition to the six chambered revolver, which he held in his hand, a box of cartridges which had been opened. 'f'wn of the chambers were empty, and the remaining four were loaded. After a very brief consultation, the jury returned a verdict of " Suicide whilst temporarily insane."
